title: India 'cockroach' leaders detained after entering barricaded protest site
text:
Leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) were detained early on Tuesday after they entered a heavily-guarded protest site and chanted slogans demanding the country's election chief resign over a controversial revision of electoral rolls.

Party founder Abhijeet Dipke shared a video showing Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das being taken away by police from Jantar Mantar, a historic Delhi observatory popular for protests.

Footage showed the two - along with others - climbing over police barricades before chanting slogans while holding the Indian flag.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's opponents allege the voter list revision benefits his party, a charge it and the Election Commission reject.

There have been days of protests demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.

Police have stepped up security across Delhi as demonstrators challenge restrictions on where protests can be held.

Early on Tuesday, Dipke, Das and Ranka all shared videos showing Das and Ranka entering Jantar Mantar.

"You cannot denotify the resistance," Dipke wrote on X.

Das also posted a message declaring that the site had been "reclaimed" and that they were being detained.

It was not immediately clear where police had taken the leaders.

Ranka later appeared on an Instagram live broadcast from a police bus alongside other detainees where they appeared cheerful and said they would not back down.

The detentions came a day after the federal home ministry announced that Jantar Mantar, long associated with public protests in Delhi, would no longer be a designated protest venue. Authorities instead identified three alternative locations where demonstrations can be held with permission.

Before the decision, the CJP had met Delhi Police officials to seek permission for a peaceful protest at Jantar Mantar and had warned that it would announce further demonstrations if it received no response.

"30 mins after we went to Delhi Police asking for a date when we can go to Jantar Mantar, Jantar Mantar was de-notified as a protest site," Ranka had earlier posted on X.

Most of the party's leadership has been in Delhi in recent days. Dipke, however, had travelled to his hometown in Maharashtra after the death of his grandmother. He was among several CJP leaders detained ahead of a planned demonstration on Saturday and was released the next day.

The CJP had called for a protest at Jantar Mantar on Saturday, but authorities imposed extensive security restrictions across the capital to prevent demonstrators from reaching the site.

Several metro stations were closed, train services were disrupted and thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed.

Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses.

title: Watch: US man eyes pumpkin world record after fifth contest win
text:
A five-time US giant pumpkin contest winner tells the BBC he'd "love" to break the world record for a second time.

Horticulture teacher Travis Gienger hauled his pumpkin from Minnesota to Half Moon Bay, California, for the annual pumpkin weighing event.

His whopping gourd took home the prize, tipping the scales at 2,389 pounds (1,083kg).

But Gienger says he's eyeing off a different prize – the world record title – which was set in England's south coast last week with a squash weighing in at 2,857 pounds (1,300kg).

As a previous holder of the world-record mantle, Gienger says he's focused on the challenge ahead.

title: South Africa's deputy police chief resigns after being charged with sexual offences
text:
South Africa's deputy police chief has resigned three weeks after he was charged with sexual offences.

A lawyer representing Lt Gen Shadrack Sibiya submitted his resignation letter at his disciplinary hearing on Monday, a police spokesperson said.

Sibiya, 59, is also accused of having links to organised crime bosses - allegations which led to him being suspended last year.

He denies those allegations, as well as charges that he sexually groomed a 16-year-old girl and raped an 18-year-old woman. He also faces a charge of human trafficking.

Sibiya says he did have sex with the 18-year-old but that it was consensual.

He has been in custody since he was arrested three weeks ago.

Police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said in a post on X that his departure from the police force was regarded as a dishonourable discharge, external because he was still facing a disciplinary case when he resigned.

The accusations that Sibiya was linked to crime bosses emerged at a major public inquiry over allegations of police corruption and collusion with criminals, known as the Madlanga Commission.

Sibiya was accused of interfering with investigations into political killings in KwaZulu-Natal province.

He was also accused of receiving a gift of cash, as well as 20 impalas, from an alleged criminal kingpin in exchange for a police contract.

He denied the allegation.

The Madlanga Commission has transfixed South Africa over the past year and unearthed widespread allegations of links between police officers and crime bosses.

It was set up by President Cyril Ramaphosa after the KwaZulu-Natal police chief held a press briefing where he accused the then Police Minister Senzo Mchunu of working with criminal gangs.

Mchunu denies the allegations against him but has been suspended.

title: Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth, BBC finds
text:
The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.

Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.

Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents.

Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant".

Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals.

Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws".

The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism.

For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club.

Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years.

The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes".

Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers.

The evidence is contained in a leak that includes thousands of documents about the oligarch's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus - which used to be a tax haven popular with Russians - between 1995 and 2022.

The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well as the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, external - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential, external investigation.

In 2022, Panorama also reported on how Abramovich had made his fortune from a corrupt deal to buy a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, selling it back to the government a decade later for billions in profit. He has previously said allegations of corruption in the deal are fal

title: Immigration agents search congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home
text:
US immigration agents have searched the home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar as part of a criminal investigation.

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents "executed a judicially authorised search warrant" for the property in the Washington DC area, a US justice department spokesperson said.

The search "is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation", the spokesperson said, but no further details were given. The US Congress is currently out of session and it is unclear if Omar was at the home.

Omar, a Democrat and outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, described the search on social media as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement".

"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar said in the post.

"This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced."

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump said he had "nothing to do" with the justice department's investigation into Omar, while describing her as a "complainer" and a "terrible person".

The Republican president said of the Somali-born congresswoman: "She comes from a country that is a non-country.

"And then she comes over here and she complains about our Constitution."

At a rally in Ohio later on Monday, Trump referred to the search of Omar's home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."

Trump went on to denigrate Somalis in the US more generally, which was greeted with chants of "deport" in the crowd, US media reported.

Omar's communications director, Jacklyn Rogers, called Monday morning's raid "an outrageous abuse of power" by the Trump administration, and said the congresswoman "has done nothing wrong".

The nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear.

An ally of Omar gave an update to the BBC World Service's Newsday programme. Asma Mohammed said: "She is doing well, she's let everyone know that she's okay and that she is used to attacks from the president but this is a new low from him."

During Monday's search, a BBC crew saw several agents at Omar's home, some carrying boxes to a van.

News of the search was first reported by Fox News, which said the investigation was about immigration paperwork filed by her late father when Omar was a child.

The timing of the raid - 22 days before the November midterm elections, which will decide the balance of power in Congress for the next two years - raised concerns from Omar's fellow Democrats.

The justice department has a longstanding policy of refraining from most enforcement action that is "likely to raise an issue or the perception" it is being brought for the purpose of affecting any election or to disadvantage a candidate.

Leading Democrats in the House of Representatives said in a statement that Omar had long been targeted with "vile personal attacks and baseless accusations" by Trump.

title: Is Zelensky right to say data centre strikes have taken down Russian bots?
text:
Claims that Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centres reduced Kremlin-linked bot networks have spread widely online, but experts have told BBC Verify there is no evidence the attacks have significantly reduced them.

Viral social media posts have claimed there has been a significant drop in influence operations in recent days, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky suggesting on Monday there was "less hate, less division and fewer provocations" online because of "fewer bots".

Russian influence operations, which promote pro-Kremlin narratives and spread disinformation, have been tracked by researchers and journalists including BBC Verify for more than a decade.

These campaigns push disinformation on to people's social media feeds on issues like the Ukraine war or post messages in support of Moscow's interests.

Ukraine has struck three of Russian tech giant Yandex's five data centres since 8 October in response to Moscow's attacks on Ukrainian internet hubs.

The second of these strikes on Thursday caused Yandex, often referred to as Russia's Google, to announce it was struggling to maintain its services.

But claims these attacks have affected Russian disinformation operations, including accounts posting supportive messages about groups including the Make American Great Again (MAGA) movement in the US and the far-right AfD party in Germany, appear to have come from a misinterpretation of data produced by tech firm Cloudflare.

Some social media users have been sharing charts of Cloudflare data which show bot activity using Yandex's network has declined.

While bots are commonly associated with fake social media accounts that may post false, divisive and inflammatory content, they are also used to automate tasks like scanning web pages so they appear on search engines.

title: The island where locals say data centres are taking their water
text:
"Water! Water!" the crowd shouted as it stormed a compound with data centres, armed with empty plastic bottles and jerry cans.

There were about 300 of them, all residents on the Indonesian island of Batam, and they were furious that the taps at home had run dry, while the data centres in the new Nongsa Digital Park seemed to have enough water to protect their machines from overheating.

"Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months... Our water supply had been reliable until the data centres came," Dewi Susanti, one of the protesters, told the BBC.

People in her village, Bakau Serip, were now depending on tanker trucks that dispensed "dirty, cloudy and smelly" water, she said.

Batam's water utility told the BBC it was working to improve supply, but did not comment on whether the disruption was linked to demand from the data centres.

But BP Batam, the agency overseeing trade and industry, blamed it on a prolonged dry spell and denied allegations from locals that water meant for homes was being channelled to data centres.

This is not the first such protest in Batam, whose shrinking reservoirs find themselves under more pressure as the island tries to transform itself into a digital hub.

Following protests in August and September, authorities told the firms opening data centres in Batam that they must build their own desalination plants instead of relying on reservoirs for freshwater.

But locals say they are increasingly concerned that they must now compete with servers for water.

"Reliable data on data centre water use in Indonesia remains scarce, partly because companies treat it as proprietary information," says Agus Hasan, a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology.

"We should build [data centres] rationally, transparently, and responsibly, and insist on seeing the numbers... [Otherwise] those kept in the dark while their taps run dry will push back, and rightly so," he adds.

A backlash has been building against data centres across the world, from the US to the UK to parts of Asia, as tech companies pour billions into AI infrastructure.

People are worried about how the huge, windowless buildings might change their neighbourhoods, the constant hum of machines, the security lights that could stay on all night, and the pressure this puts on water and energy resources.

While electricity powers the centres, the water keeps the servers from frying – engineers deploy elaborate cooling systems, which consume a lot of water.

Research in the US suggests a typical data centre consumes around 300,000 gallons of water a day, or about as much as 1,000 US households. A larger, 50MW facility could take as much water as 2,200 households per day, and enough electricity to power 22,000 homes, according to Malaysia's central bank.

It's unclear how much water or electricity the data centres in Batam are consuming.

title: Boardroom feud tests trusted Indian business empire
text:
Before dawn breaks over Mumbai, Mansi Kadam begins preparing vada pav, a savoury snack synonymous with the western Indian city, for the day's customers. One ingredient is non-negotiable: Tata salt.

When asked whether she would ever consider switching brands, her reply is a reminder of an old Hindi ad jingle, "If it's salt, it has to be Tata."

She knows little about the developments unfolding in the boardroom of the Tata group, one of India's oldest and most influential business empires that makes everything from salt to software.

But her instinctive loyalty points to a question confronting the group: Can one of India's most trusted brands remain insulated from a public battle over power, governance and control?

A recent public disagreement between the board of Tata Sons, the holding company of the Tata group and Tata Trusts, its principal shareholder, has put a spotlight on the conglomerate.

At the centre of the dispute are two issues - the proposed public listing of Tata Sons and the reappointment of chairman N Chandrasekaran. Most of the Tata Sons board, including its biggest minority shareholder SP Group, supported the decisions.

But Noel Tata, chairman of majority shareholder Tata Trusts, has opposed both resolutions. He maintains that a public listing would dilute the group's philanthropic ethos and is likely to get both decisions overturned at its annual general meeting.

"When we say this is a governance crisis, it's a misalignment of interests between the board [of Tata Sons] and the shareholders [Tata Trusts]," Shriram Subramanian, head of independent corporate governance firm InGovern Research, told the BBC.

While he does not expect the brand's image to be affected immediately, he flags concerns over the leadership's ability to navigate the challenges.

Disagreements within the Tata Group have been simmering since the death of former chairman Ratan Tata - Noel Tata's half-brother who designated him successor after his death - in 2024. For many Indians, Ratan Tata's philanthropy and leadership had become inseparable from the brand. His death triggered widespread mourning and experts say it left a leadership void in the group's image with the public.

The Tata group has topped India's most valuable brand list by valuation consultancy Brand Finance since 2018, according to the group's website.

Tata Sons, the business entity, is described by the group as the "fastener keeping the many disparate elements of the whole together".

Tata Trusts, which represents seven philanthropic trusts that own the majority stake in the group, is widely regarded as its moral compass, guiding the businesses on social impact and philanthropy.

For many Indians, both the entities together make up what most companies cannot buy - trust.

Now with these entities in rival corners, that is coming under strain.

title: Death threats and isolation - the cost of fighting sexual violence in Iraq
text:
This story contains details of sexual violence which some readers may find upsetting

"Get out of the car!" screams a woman, accusing a driver of exposing himself and making obscene comments as she walked by. She is filming the scene in a busy Baghdad street on her phone, and the camera captures him resisting her attempts to open the door as she confronts him.

The video can be seen, with others like it, on the Instagram page of Iraqi women's rights activist Sarah Jassim. She posts them on behalf of women who complain about sexual abuse and harassment by Iraqi men and boys.

"Your camera is your weapon," she tells the BBC. "It's a way to document evidence in case a woman decides to sue her harasser, or at least it is a means to shame him."

One of the videos she posted led to the arrest of the alleged perpetrator, a policeman accused of harassing schoolgirls, she says.

Jassim says posting the videos is risky both for herself and for the women concerned. We have spoken to numerous victims of sexual abuse in Iraq who say that society often blames the victim.

"I have received death threats, and I have also been threatened with acid attacks," Jassim says. "I have been accused of inciting public indecency, because I encourage women to speak in a society that expects us to be silent."

She now barely leaves home, for her own safety, and instead spends hours playing with her dog.

There is a need for stricter laws, she argues, including laws that explicitly criminalise "harassment" and "gender-based violence" - terms that are currently absent from the penal code.

"Recognising the problem is the best way to address it," she says. "We need protection, abusers have to be deterred."

Many Iraqi women have told the BBC they felt failed by the justice and police systems. Pursuing legal action against a harasser or a rapist is a long path in Iraq, with complicated procedures, and uncertain results, according to a number of activists and lawyers we have spoken to.

Violence against women and girls in Iraq is "widespread and under-reported," according to a report in May by a UN committee on discrimination against women, which called for stronger legislation.

Among dozens of recommendations, it urged the authorities to repeal "discriminatory" laws that exonerate rapists if they marry their victims, and allow reduced sentences for murder in cases where a perpetrator was carrying out a so-called "honour killing".

Amal - not her real name - has been battling in court for about five years. She accuses her ex-husband of repeatedly raping their daughter - who was under 18 at the time - at gunpoint.

She recalls her daughter's harrowing account of the incident, when she says the father walked into the girl's room and laid his weapon on her bed. She says he told her: "No-one will hear you if I kill you."

title: Where the US midterm elections will be won and lost
text:
Americans head to the polls on 3 November to decide how the rest of Donald Trump's presidency will play out.

Thousands of races are taking place across the US, at different levels of government. But the main event for voters will be electing members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers that make up Congress.

Both of them are currently controlled by the Republicans, the president's party. The success or failure of Trump's final two years in office could rest on the outcome.

Here's our visual guide to where the battle for power will be won and lost - from approval ratings, to key races and issues and the huge amount of money being spent.

One of the reasons the opposition Democrats have a chance to take back Congress is the president's low approval rating, which is a good indicator for how well his party could perform.

He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but it quickly fell into the 40s.

It was hovering around 42% when Trump decided to launch air strikes with Israel against Iran at the end of February this year but it fell below 40% shortly afterwards. It is currently sitting at about 37%.

Eight years ago, Trump's approval rating was significantly higher at this point in his first term, at 43%. Joe Biden's at the same point in his term was at 40%. In both cases, the sitting president lost control of the House in the midterms but kept hold of the Senate.

But Trump's poor ratings help explain why Democrats are hopeful of winning both chambers of Congress and why they are setting their sights on states that Republicans have won consistently in recent years.

Members of the House serve a two-year term so all 435 seats are up for election in November.

But most districts are not considered competitive because the party that holds them has such solid support that there is only one likely winner.

The Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, suggests that just 21 districts are "toss-ups" that could be won by either party.

But winning a majority is no easy task for the Democrats.

They need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where polls suggest the race is tighter than Democrats would like between Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, and his Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent.

And they would also need to pick up seats in states that Trump won by double-digits in 2024, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio.

But polls suggest they have a chance, even in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.

Trump pledged to "end inflation and make America affordable again" in his 2024 election campaign but the cost of living crisis is proving to be the key issue for voters.

title: BBC's Orla Guerin travels with Yemen's southern national security forces through desert battlefield
text:
On Yemen's desert battlefield a war with global consequences is being waged.

The BBC's Orla Guerin saw the impact firsthand when she travelled with southern national security forces to frontline positions where they've been battling Houthi fighters.

Yemen's civil war over expanses of desert land has had devastating consequences for civilians and fighters.

One military hospital in Aden reported more than 50 casualties arriving in a single day – many with gunshot wounds, and several needing amputations.

title: French fridge fright: Why supermarkets have become target for hackers
text:
Hundreds of French supermarkets have suffered unprecedented cyberattacks resulting in tonnes of food perishing and raising fears about the vulnerabilities of food systems to advanced technology.

The attacks, which appeared to target internet-linked refrigeration systems manufactured by a Danish company, raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F) at more than 500 shops and supermarkets across the country. Supermarkets confirmed the attacks on Monday.

France’s cybersecurity agency has advised companies operating affected freezer models to immediately disconnect them from the internet – or restrict access to them – and to perform software updates.

It is unclear who may have been behind the attacks, but authorities say they have now launched an investigation.

Here’s what we know:

What happened?

Hackers gained internet access to the refrigeration systems and remotely cranked up temperatures in freezers and fridges to 50C during the night when shops were closed. Millions of euros worth of food was spoiled, according to retailers. In some cases, the raised temperatures sparked fires or melted equipment.

French supermarket groups E-Leclerc, Intermarche, Carrefour, Monoprix and Cooperative U were all hit.

At least 300 of Intermarche’s stores and its Netto brand were affected. Cooperative U said more than 100 of its supermarkets were targeted, while Carrefour said 80 supermarkets were affected and Monoprix reported that about 5 percent of its roughly 490 stores were hit.

Officials are still investigating who launched the attack and how it was carried out. French TV channel BFM reported that the attackers appeared to have remotely triggered a forced defrosting option in the refrigeration systems.

The systems targeted are built by Danish manufacturer Danfoss, according to France’s government cybersecurity agency. The refrigeration models attacked included the AK-SM800 and AK-SC355.

Danfoss told the AFP news agency that most of the affected control systems were “legacy” products that had “outdated firmware”. The company said it had previously advised supermarkets to update them.

AFP also reported that officials are liaising with other European countries which may have been affected.

It is unclear exactly how much food has been lost. The attacks come after President Emmanuel Macron ordered last month that the country’s critical infrastructure be protected from Russian “hybrid attacks”.

title: Trump’s diesel deal opens a new rift with Europe over Ukraine
text:
Russia has claimed it can supply even more diesel to the global market than the quantities agreed with United States President Donald Trump.

“By the end of the year, we could reach supply volumes of 3.5 million tonnes per month to global markets, just as was the case before the crisis,” Alexander Novak, Russian deputy prime minister, told the news programme Vesti on Monday.

President Vladimir Putin and Trump spoke on Friday on an agreement expected to bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel to global markets in October, half a million tonnes in November, and a million tonnes in December.

“Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump posted.

But experts are sceptical, and the move has opened a rift between the US and Europe on the Ukraine war.

Kostis Stambolis, executive director of the Institute of Energy for South-East Europe (IENE), described the US move as “purely political” and designed to put Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a corner.

Trump wants to signal that the US has “no problem with Russia”, unlike Europe, he said.

“Russia produces 5.8 million tonnes of diesel a month. Two million are likely to be available for export,” he added.

Europe has reacted to the diesel deal by backing Ukraine, whose war funding will be “front and centre” of this week’s European Council summit, European Commission President Ursula Von Der Leyen said on Sunday.

Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen on Monday called on Europeans to ban all tourist visas to Russians.

Stambolis believes Trump was leveraging European weakness to shift its position on Ukraine.

“About 30 European refineries have closed in the past 15 years for environmental reasons, because they have to pay to emit greenhouse gases,” he said, referring to Europe’s Emissions Trading Scheme, “so now Europe is not self-sufficient in products”.

Trump is showing the Europeans “he doesn’t want to deal with Europe and to hell with them … This is opening the rift between the US and the EU further,” said Stambolis.

Ukraine says it has destroyed roughly half of Russia’s refining capacity, forcing Moscow to stop exporting lucrative petroleum products which help it to finance its war.

It has also bombed Russian tankers carrying crude oil to global markets.

title: Iran sees ‘false flag’ operations after UK blames IRGC for airbase incident
text:
Tehran, Iran – Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has condemned the United Kingdom’s attribution of an alleged plot near a military airbase in the town of Fairford to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which it views as part of a greater Western effort.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Parliament on Monday that the suspected plot last month against the Royal Air Force base was “highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran” and “almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard”.

title: Iran threatens Gulf data centres: How exposed is the region’s internet?
text:
Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, has warned that cables, data centres and artificial intelligence (AI) facilities across the region could be attacked if war with the United States erupts again.

The warning comes as the capture of Yemeni territory along the Red Sea coastline last month by the Iran-backed Houthis has raised concerns over the safety of internet cables linking Europe and Asia. Fierce fighting is under way between Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Houthis at several locations, including Bab al-Mandeb, through which nearly one-fifth of global internet traffic passes.

Recommended Stories

Data centres and US business interests were hit in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates during the US-Israel war on Iran. Tehran said these attacks were in response to US attacks on Iranian civilian installations.

Active hostilities have largely ended since the June memorandum of understanding between Iran and the US, but attacks on ships passing through the global oil chokepoint – the Strait of Hormuz – have continued.

So how exposed is the region’s internet? Here’s what you need to know:

Why are data centres and internet cables vulnerable?

Because so much data travels through a few narrow routes.

More than 90 percent of data capacity between Europe and Asia passes through cables under the Red Sea, according to estimates by the research firm TeleGeography.

They enter the sea through Bab al-Mandeb, a strait about 26km (16 miles) wide at its narrowest, one of the busiest maritime routes connecting Europe to Asia.

Cables can be cut by anchors or sabotage, and repairs in a war zone need permits and safety guarantees.

Data centres, which run banking apps and cloud services, are large, fixed targets.

“An attack does not necessarily need to destroy the servers themselves to render an entire facility inoperable,” Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer in security studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.

Data centres depend on uninterrupted electricity, cooling and telecommunications, he said, while undersea cables “are difficult to protect continuously and disruption can affect several countries simultaneously”.

Yes, repeatedly since the war began in February.

On March 11, the semi-official Tasnim news agency said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has published a list of “Iran’s new targets”, including cloud infrastructure belonging to Google, Microsoft and Oracle in Israel and some Gulf states.

title: Rwanda to host a Grand Prix in 2030s as Formula One returns to Africa
text:
Kigali, Rwanda – Formula One will return to Africa after a decades-long absence, with Rwanda scheduled to host a Grand Prix in the early 2030s.

Rwandan President Paul Kagame made the announcement during a ceremony attended by Formula One President and CEO Stefano Domenicali and FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem in Kigali on Tuesday.

“Rwanda has been working very hard towards hosting the African Grand Prix,” Kagame said. He referred to it a “partnership” that was long overdue but “a milestone for the continent”.

The East African nation has secured a 10-year deal to bring Formula One back to the continent for the first time since 1993, with the inaugural race projected for the early 2030s.

The Grand Prix will be held near Kigali, with former Austrian motorsport driver Alex Wurz’s racetrack design firm in charge of designing the new circuit.

It will be built near the Bugesera international airport, 40 kilometres (24.8 miles) south of Kigali.

The circuit will stretch over six kilometres, with 17 corners and an anti-clockwise layout. Designed to follow the natural terrain, it will feature an elevation gain of 197 metres per lap. The track will be developed to FIA Grade 1 standards and is expected to host other motorsport competitions and major events.

Kagame emphasised that “Rwanda is happy and excited to be part of a journey that will change how Africa is conceived by the world of sports”.

‘Missing piece’

Mohammed Ben Sulayem, president of the sport’s governing body, hailed Formula One’s return to Africa as “a moment of immense pride”, adding that it opened “a new chapter in the history of Formula One”.

Formula One chief Domenicali termed Africa “the missing piece” in the championship’s global footprint.

In December 2024, the Rwandan president announced the country’s bid to host a Formula One Grand Prix during an address to the FIA General Assembly in Kigali.

Lewis Hamilton, Formula One’s most successful driver with seven world titles and 106 Grand Prix wins, has been a leading proponent of the competition’s return to Africa.

At last week’s Singapore Grand Prix, Hamilton was asked about the prospects of an F1 race in Africa and reiterated his stance, saying: “We need to have a Grand Prix in Africa.”

“It is, for me, the most important continent, to be honest, the most beautiful continent,” the Ferrari driver said. “We’re on all the other continents but that one and there should be no reason for it.”

The British driver is known to have advocated for an F1 race in Africa for years and has publicly urged F1’s Domenicali to add a race in Africa.

“It is something I’ve been pushing for in the background, and Stefano has been amazing,” Hamilton said last week.

“He’s flown to Africa so many times over the last couple of years, speaking to lots and lots of different people, so I hope that he has some news for me soon.”

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, the reigning world champion, also expressed his excitement.

title: Deadly Houthi attacks in Yemen’s Taiz as government forces advance in Marib
text:
Yemeni government forces say they have made strategic advances into the Marib governorate in north-central Yemen as they push on with operation “Dawn of Yemen”.

The offensive by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, launched just over a week ago, comes after major gains by the Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God, in September, when it swept along the country’s Red Sea coast, capturing the strategic port city of Mocha and territory around the Bab al-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important shipping routes.

Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, said operation Dawn of Yemen aimed to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the group has controlled since 2014, when the war first started.

Meanwhile, intense clashes and Houthi shelling on residential neighbourhoods in Taiz in the southwest of the country have caused dozens of civilian casualties.

Operation Dawn of Yemen

In the northwest of Marib governorate, a military source told Al Jazeera that government troops have successfully taken control of strategic, commanding heights surrounding the strategic Maas camp facility in the Medghal district. The source noted this followed intensive attacks that had breached the Houthi group’s fortifications.

On the southern front, forces from the Saba and Bayhan axes announced the capture of the al-Muqailat and Jabal Zajjar positions north of the Harib district. Government forces claimed the fierce clashes resulted in the Houthis retreating and suffering human and material losses.

This field progress coincided with continued violent battles along the front lines in the north and south of Marib. Government forces launched concentrated strikes using warplanes, drones, artillery and rocket launchers, targeting Houthi military positions and reinforcements.

The armed forces’ media centre published footage it said documented drone attacks on Houthi military barracks and vehicles within the scope of the third military region’s operations, noting the destruction of multiple combat vehicles and equipment.

Above: Footage from the battles within the operational theatre of the seventh military region north of Marib: Media centre of armed forces.

Military spokesperson Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili announced on Monday that operations have involved 1,879 precise strikes, neutralising 950 Houthi fighters and destroying 380 military vehicles.

Meanwhile, Houthi-affiliated media reported that air strikes targeted Kamaran Island and the al-Qanawis district in the coastal Hodeidah governorate along the Red Sea and the Harf Sufyan district in Amran, western-central Yemen.

Escalation in Taiz

title: African Union holds Kigali talks as fighting continues in eastern DRC
text:
Kigali, Rwanda – The African Union (AU) has held consultations in Kigali, Rwanda, as part of efforts to advance the peace process in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where fighting continues despite diplomatic initiatives to end the conflict.

The consultations, held on October 6, focused on implementing the Washington Peace Agreement, security arrangements, the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration of fighters, refugee protection and regional economic cooperation, the AU said in a statement.

The delegation comprised former Ethiopian President Sahle-Work Zewde, former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta and former Botswana President Mokgweetsi Masisi. Zewde is the deputy chairperson of the AU Panel of Facilitators for the eastern DRC peace process.

From Goma to Kigali

The Kigali consultations followed meetings in Goma, eastern DRC, on October 5. According to the AU, the delegation met representatives of the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM+) and the Alliance Fleuve Congo/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23).

Following the Goma meetings, the AU panel called for respect for ceasefire commitments, cooperation with verification mechanisms and restraint from actions that could undermine the peace process. It also stressed the need to protect civilians, ensure safe humanitarian access and prevent sexual and gender-based violence.

In Kigali, the facilitators held separate consultations with Rwandan officials and representatives of regional institutions. The AU said the discussions covered security commitments, the protection of refugees and returnees, and regional economic cooperation, including mineral traceability, cross-border trade, energy and infrastructure.

The facilitators said they would continue their engagements in Kinshasa as part of efforts to support dialogue and advance the peace process.

Two agreements, separate negotiations

The consultations come amid parallel diplomatic efforts to address the conflict. The Washington Peace Agreement, signed by the DRC and Rwanda on June 27, 2025, includes security commitments intended to address concerns over armed groups and the presence of forces in eastern DRC.

Implementation remains a central issue. At a meeting of the agreement’s Joint Oversight Committee in June 2026, the parties expressed concern over escalating fighting and called for the agreement to be fully implemented, including commitments concerning the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) and the disengagement of forces.

title: Australia bowl out South Africa to win first cricket Test in Durban
text:
Australia’s pace bowler Josh Hazlewood has bowled his side to a 214-run ⁠⁠victory over South Africa on the last ⁠⁠day of the first cricket Test match at the Kingsmead Stadium in Durban.

The hosts’ resistance ended before tea on Tuesday as they were dismissed for 206.

Hazlewood took 6-49 ⁠⁠as Australia bagged the six wickets they needed on the last day to go 1-0 up in the three-match series.

He struck twice in one over with the new ball after ⁠⁠already having taken two wickets on Monday and then breaking through South Africa’s stoic early fightback.

The 35-year-old Hazlewood also removed the last batsman to ensure the victory in the first clash between the teams since South Africa upset Australia in last year’s World Test Championship final at ‌‌Lord’s in London.

South Africa held out for the first 110 minutes of Tuesday’s play before a legside delivery from Hazlewood was edged by Wiaan Mulder and snagged by a diving catch from wicketkeeper Alex Carey.

Mulder and Aiden Markram resumed at 102-4 overnight, and the pair extended the fifth-wicket partnership to a patient 69 runs off 205 balls before Hazlewood’s breakthrough, with Mulder making 29.

Part-time spinner Matt Renshaw, who was the man of the match ⁠⁠for Australia with the bat, then took a second Test wicket ⁠⁠when Kyle Verreynne quickly followed Mulder back to the change room with a reckless shot that saw him caught at slip by Steve Smith without scoring.

South Africa were 166-6 at lunch and added 25 runs before the new ⁠⁠ball was taken, but crumbled quickly thereafter.

Marco Jansen was bowled by Hazlewood for 35 and three balls later Simon Harmer followed as he brushed ⁠⁠the ball through to Carey with his glove.

Markram then ⁠⁠fell after a patient 75 off 237 balls, edging Mitch Starc’s delivery off his pads to be caught behind, but was only given out after a television review.

Hazlewood then completed the win as tailender Anrich Nortje popped up the ball ‌‌to short midwicket for Nathan Lyon to catch.

Former Australia captain Smith, who did not field in Monday’s late session after a blow to the head while batting, returned to action on ‌‌Tuesday.

“Steve ‌‌Smith has undergone a series of clinical assessments over the past 24 hours in accordance with Cricket Australia’s concussion protocols and has been cleared to take the field this morning,” a statement said.

title: Yemeni families’ search for missing loved ones hindered by new fighting
text:
Sanaa, Yemen – In 2020, 18-year-old Munif bid farewell to his family and left his home in Sanaa to fight with the Houthis on the front lines of Yemen’s civil war

After six months, all of his comrades went back to their families, but Munif never returned home.

More than six years have passed, and Munif’s family, who asked to use just his first name for security reasons, are still searching for answers about his fate.

He is one of hundreds of people who have disappeared in Yemen since war broke out in September 2014, when the Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God) – captured the capital and forced the internationally-recognised government to flee south.

“Ten other men from our village joined the front line on the Saudi-Yemen border. All of them came back. We asked them about my brother’s whereabouts, but none could tell us where he had gone,” said Mohammed, Munif’s brother. “A definite answer about his status would be a relief for the entire family.”

There were hopes that a truce in 2022 between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and Iran-aligned Houthis could help families begin their search for their missing loved ones.

Since July this year, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has received more than 1,800 tracing requests from families looking for missing relatives in Yemen.

But the resumption of fighting in July has halted this search for many families, who are trying to find out if loved ones have been detained, injured, killed, or simply lost in records, due to displacement or desertion.

After careful consideration, Mohammed believes there are two possible outcomes for his brother, Munif.

“He might have been hit by an air strike, leaving no trace of his body, or perhaps he was captured, and he remains in captivity,” Mohammed said.

If Munif was killed in an explosion, finding a body part that could be identified would bring the family some relief. But the family is still hoping for the latter scenario, and that Munif is being held captive by government forces.

“We would have accepted his death, adjusted to the loss, and forgotten my brother’s possible return. We just need to know what happened to him,” he said.

“We have heard about some fighters who were believed to be dead, and their families accepted the news of their deaths and mourned them. However, they emerged alive after years of captivity. So, Munif may still be alive.”

Both sides have held many prisoners of war over the decade-long conflict, but the number of captives remains uncertain.

title: How protests have shaped India: From anti-Hindi agitation to farm laws
text:
New Delhi, India – Central parts of the Indian capital have been flooded in recent days with thousands of armed personnel, chasing down young protesters demanding the resignation of the country’s chief election commissioner (CEC) and struggling to secure a place to stage a sit-in in New Delhi.

Since last week, several student organisations and a wide spectrum of opposition parties have been engaged in a tactical tug-of-war, with tens of thousands turning up on Monday, far outnumbering police personnel.

Protesters are demanding sweeping reforms and the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar after revelations of election irregularities. The agitation marks the latest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s grip on power, after his education minister was forced out by the same group of demonstrators less than three months ago.

The Modi government has tried to portray protesters as representing antinational interests, working to slow down India’s growth or even to enable its breakup.

But India, the world’s most populous country, has had a long history of street protests, from its freedom struggle against the British Empire to waves of movements during the 79 years of the Indian republic that have shaped its modern identity.

“Time and again the government [of the day] has opposed these protests, [and] at times engaged with them critically,” Rasheed Kidwai, a political analyst in New Delhi and former journalist, told Al Jazeera. “But protests have run centrally through India’s story all along.”

Here is a look at major street protests in India and how they often forced powerful governments and leaders to yield.

Anti-Hindi agitations (1965)

India’s newly-formed constitution envisaged Hindi replacing English as the central government’s official language after a 15-year transition, ending on January 26, 1965. Many people in southern India, particularly Tamil speakers in the then Madras state (now Tamil Nadu), feared that this would sideline them in government employment, civil service examinations and dealings with the central administration.

For the federal government of a vast and diverse country, the idea of one common official language of communication was attractive as a tool of unification. But for many of the ancient societies that had agreed to come together under the Indian Union, this led to fears of cultural domination by the Hindi-speaking north of the country.

Demonstrations by several student organisations, opposing the imposition of Hindi, broke out, often leading to clashes with the police.

The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), a regional political party advocating Tamil nationalism, led by CN Annadurai and M Karunanidhi, spearheaded the protests. In January 1965, Annadurai was arrested on the eve of an anti-Hindi agitation. Two young supporters immolated themselves, and Hindi books were burned.

title: ‘My son was killed’: France faces backlash over police firearms bill
text:
Paris, France – Issam El Khalfaoui’s teenage son Souhail was shot and killed by a police officer in 2021 in Marseille.

“When my son was killed during a police traffic stop, we realised how difficult it was to bring the truth to light. The police and the justice system took different actions to cover up the evidence. We realised that this was a deeply systemic issue,” El Khalfaoui told Al Jazeera. “The IGPN [National Police] lost the video that captured my son’s murder. The witnesses were not interviewed, and the case file completely disappeared from the court. That is the reality.”

France has one of the highest numbers of fatal police shootings in Western Europe. At least 69 people were killed by police or gendarmerie officers in 2024, compared with 49 in 2023 and 50 in 2022.

Now, French police are again facing scrutiny, this time over their tactics during clashes in education protests. A 15-year-old lost a hand from a police stun grenade, and another officer threw a tear gas canister at close range, shattering a 14-year-old’s jaw and several teeth. The use of stun grenades has since been halted. Authorities say 700 police have also been injured.

The unrest comes as a controversial bill that would presume police officers acted in self-defence when using firearms faces a vote in the Senate.

Khalfaoui launched a petition against the draft law that received more than 700,000 signatures. The measure, which critics describe as a “licence to kill”, was approved by the National Assembly in July.

Several advocacy groups, including Stop State Violence (SAVE), the Human Rights League (LDH) and Amnesty International, as well as left-wing lawmakers, organised protests in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Toulouse, which drew nearly 50,000 people on September 20.

Under the proposed law, police officers and gendarmes would be presumed to have acted in self-defence if they used weapons in the line of duty, placing the burden of proof on the complainant.

For El Khalfaoui, who co-founded SAVE after his 19-year-old son’s death, passing the law would only increase the police’s strength.

“In France, there has been a seizure of power by police unions,” El Khalfaoui said. “There’s a militarisation of the police that has no equivalent in Europe, and resources have been allocated to the police to ensure the police’s loyalty to the government.”

The draft law could entrench a sense of impunity, El Khalfaoui noted.

“It will be impossible to refute this presumption of self-defence,” he said.

title: Activist Greta Thunberg joins French student protests
text:
Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg has joined the French student protests as more demonstrations calling for better conditions at education facilities are expected nationwide.

Thunberg arrived at Paul Eluard high school in the heart of the movement in the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis on Tuesday morning and stood among the students demonstrating.

Recommended Stories

list 2 of 3Stolen Renoir paintings found behind wall in France following arrests

list 3 of 3Hundreds of supermarkets in France hit by ‘unprecedented’ cyberattack

end of list

“Young people are not being included in the conversation. Our future is being robbed away from us,” Thunberg told the AFP news agency.

Lawyers in robes had also formed a human chain to protect teens following numerous allegations of police brutality at demonstrations.

The protests started late last month as students demanded improvements on a range of issues, including the state of school buildings, a lack of teachers, crowded class schedules and other problems in the education system.

Students have piled up bins and erected security barriers outside hundreds of schools across the country.

Last Thursday, more than 70,000 people took to the streets in the latest major protest event.

Tuesday’s demonstration, backed by unions and a left-wing opposition party, France Unbowed, included a march through Paris and marches in other cities. Pupils clustered outside the doors of several schools in the morning hours, brandishing placards and megaphones and chanting slogans, and marches were planned later in the day.

The university student union, l’Union, said on X: “They’re not listening to us, so we’re going to them.”

Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on France Inter on Tuesday morning that about 200 schools were closed, which was “fewer than last week”, adding that some near protest routes were closing to avoid damage.

The Ministry of National Education also said eight members of teaching staff were injured on Monday, mostly in the Paris region and cities of Bordeaux and Lyon, due to the protests.

On Monday, a 19-year-old graphic design student in Paris, Leo, told AFP that “Students aren’t being heard enough … not their proposals to authorities and elected officials.”

He added that the protesters, many being minors, were “disturbed by the level of repression never before seen for a student movement”.

Tuesday’s demonstrations supporting the students are expected to be followed on Saturday by wider public rallies against the rising cost of living.

On Monday, French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters at a car show that he urged protesters to exercise restraint.

“These are issues that deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect,” Macron said.

According to the Ministry of Justice, more than 6,800 people, mainly minors, have been taken into police custody over the course of the protests.

title: One killed, several injured in Georgia rollercoaster ‘incident’
text:
A person has died and several others have been injured in an incident involving a rollercoaster at an amusement park in the state of Georgia in the United States.

The incident happened on Monday at the Six Flags amusement park, about 15 miles (24km) northwest of Atlanta.

Officials are investigating the death but have yet to confirm its nature or how the others were injured.

Images and videos have been circulating online that appear to show a man who seems to have been ejected from his seat and landed on the ground.

Al Jazeera has not independently verified the footage.

Six Flags has since closed nine rollercoasters at six of its parks “out of an abundance of caution”, a spokesperson said, adding that they are similar to the one involved in the incident.

Police and the company did not name the ride, but local TV footage showed passengers being escorted off the Goliath rollercoaster, which stopped halfway through the ride.

Witnesses also told local station 11Alive that they saw a man land on the roof of a haunted house attraction; those accounts have also not been verified.

Six Flags said it was “deeply saddened by the guest incident” and that it was supporting guests and staff affected.

Lisa Cupid, chairwoman of the Cobb County board of commissioners, said she “cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today”.

The Goliath rollercoaster opened in 2006 and reaches 70mph (113km/h) at a height of 200 feet (61 metres), according to the company’s website.

This marks at least the seventh death at the park, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park accidents. Earlier, one occurred on Goliath in 2006, after a man likely had a heart attack on the ride.

About two weeks ago, Six Flags Magic Mountain in California announced it would retire its X2 rollercoaster after more than 100 people reportedly sustained brain injuries while riding it.

The company said the ride had passed safety tests, but it was closing it regardless because it’s just the “right thing to do”.

In 2021, Israel designated six Palestinian organisations, including Addameer and the Union of Palestinian Women’s Committees, as “terrorist” organisations.

What’s the ongoing story: New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar is no longer a “designated site” for protests, the Delhi Police announced on Monday (October 12). Three new venues — the Ramlila Ground in Central Delhi, the Burari Ground in North Delhi, and the CBD Ground in East Delhi — have been designated as sites for organising protests and demonstrations.

Key Points to Ponder:

• What is the significance of Jantar Mantar in India’s democratic and political landscape?

• What are the constitutional basis of the right to peaceful protest in India?

• How did Jantar Mantar emerge as principal hub for public demonstrations?

• What is the difference between the right to protest and the right to assemble peacefully?

• How can protest sites be designated?

• In a constitutional democracy, should the state prioritise the convenience of administration or the effective exercise of citizens’ right to peaceful protest?

• ‘The geography of dissent is an important dimension of democratic governance’— Discuss how the location, accessibility and visibility of public spaces influence the relationship between citizens and the state.

• A notice issued by Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar said: “[The] Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, had constituted a Committee to examine alternative proper venues for citizen’s right for organizing protest/demonstrations in place of the existing ‘designated site’. • This comes after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a social media satire page turned pressure group, and several other organisations including Left-affiliated groups had called upon citizens to protest at different spots across Central Delhi, including Jantar Mantar, on Saturday and Sunday. The authorities, meanwhile, deployed thousands of police personnel to secure the surrounding areas and detained thousands of protesters over two days.

title: Niti Taylor reveals a director’s casting couch demand made her quit films: ‘I told no one’
text:
Niti Taylor recalls casting couch experience with a director

Niti Taylor said the director of her first Telugu film contacted her about working together on another project. However, the conversation took an uncomfortable turn when he allegedly made a sexual demand.

“The director who did the first film with me called me for another movie when we were done with it. Then he said, ‘but you will have to sleep with me for it this time.’ You do not realise, you do not know how to react. I just cut the call, I blocked his number, I called up my mom, and I’m like, imagine that buddha, old man,” she said.

The actor recalled being too stunned by the proposition to confront the director.

Niti also suggested that she had previously seen the director around other female actors but had not expected him to approach her with a similar demand. The experience changed her outlook on working in films.

“I saw him with other chicks and stuff like that. I never knew when he would try this with me. That’s when I decided I would never do any movies ever again. I was just taken aback, and I only blocked him. I did not tell this to anyone because I was zapped,” Niti explained.

She did not reveal the director’s identity during the conversation.

Niti Taylor’s Telugu film career

Niti Taylor entered Telugu cinema in 2012 with Mem Vayasuku Vacham, directed by Trinadha Rao Nakkina and starring Tanish in the lead role. Produced by Bekkam Venugopal, the film performed well commercially and marked the beginning of her brief stint in the Telugu film industry.

She followed it with Pelli Pustakam in 2013. Directed by Ramakrishna Machakanti, the film featured Rahul Ravindran as the male lead. Unlike her debut, the movie failed to find success at the box office and received a largely negative response from critics.

Niti did not return to films after these three Telugu projects.

Niti Taylor’s television career

Niti Taylor made her television debut at the age of 15 with the Hindi show Pyaar Ka Bandhan, before gaining wider recognition with the youth drama Kaisi Yeh Yaariaan in 2014.

Over the years, she appeared in several television projects, including Bade Achhe Lagte Hain 2. More recently, she participated in the reality show Alliance, where she emerged as a semi-finalist. Mini Mathur won the competition.

What is behind Seoul’s need for secrecy?

There are several reasons why South Korea wanted to keep the POW transfer secret, Erwin Tan, a professor of international politics at Hankuk University, told DW.

“The first was that revealing that the POWs had been repatriated to South Korea would result in Pyongyang retaliating against the families of the men for surrendering,” Tan said.

“Seoul also wanted to maintain a channel for communication with Pyongyang,” Tan said. “This is a major consideration for the left-leaning wing of Korean politics, which includes President Lee and has historically favored seeking rapprochement with the North.”

Kim Sang-woo, a former politician with the left-leaning South Korean Congress for New Politics and now a member of the board of the Kim Dae-jung Peace Foundation, agrees that the South Korean government wanted to avoid “friction” with the North.

But Kim pointed out that it was always very likely that both Moscow and Pyongyang would find out about the transfer sooner or later and that Lee was being criticized in some quarters at home for appearing weak.

“There is criticism that Lee’s administration is effectively appeasing the North, that it has become too soft, and that is a very worrisome situation,” Kim said. Yet he admits to being surprised at how quickly the issue escalated.

“I think Lee was very angry that he was publicly being accused of lying about the agreement and it rapidly grew into a very messy confrontation,” he said.

Has Zelenskyy’s approach backfired?

While it is unclear why Zelenskyy used his high-profile UN speech to announce the repatriation of the two POWs, Kim believes it may have been a calculated move to win more support from Seoul.

Kyiv could have carried out a prisoner swap with the Russians and won the freedom of some of its own men in return.

“I am excited to begin a new chapter in my life with the Delhi Capitals. I have an old association with the franchise and know the owners well, which makes this a special opportunity for me. title: Israel and the US see Navi Pillay’s Peace Prize as a verdict on them — rightly so
text:
Advertisement

Israel’s reaction to this year’s prize warrants a return to these examples. “The Nobel Prize committee has lost its moral compass,” PM Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said after the award went to Navi Pillay, a former judge of the International Criminal Court (ICC), “for her efforts to promote peace and international law”. I read the Nobel Committee’s announcement in full. It does not mention Israel by name, and unlike the above-cited dissidents who were targeted by their own governments, Pillay isn’t even Israeli.

What, then, explains the angry reaction from Israel, and from the United States and its president Donald Trump, who claimed to have “never heard” of Pillay? In September 2025, a UN commission that she was chairing at the time concluded that Israeli authorities and security forces had “committed genocide” against Palestinians in Gaza. The Committee’s announcement included that commission on Pillay’s list of contributions, and Israel and the US heard the rest for themselves.

Understandably so. By honouring Pillay, the Committee has recognised the validity of an investigation that has placed Israel’s conduct in Gaza under the harshest possible international scrutiny. It has lent legitimacy to the findings that have challenged Israel’s account of its military campaign, which Israel and the US have sought to discredit. And it has affirmed the importance of the institutions and individuals who pursue accountability, even when their findings are unwelcome to powerful states.

Speaking of the powerful, look at Washington’s response. Right after Pillay was honoured, the Trump administration announced new sanctions against the ICC. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US would “ban transactions with this rogue court”. This, despite the fact that the ICC and the UN commission that Pillay chaired are separate institutions, and the Nobel Committee’s announcement does not mention the US at all.

The Israeli-American reaction was always likely to seek to discredit Pillay. But if her career demonstrates anything, it is her relentless pursuit of accountability, most famously in the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda prosecuting those responsible for the 1994 genocide. She is also serving as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice in the case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar over allegations of genocide against the Rohingya. One can hardly be blamed for putting faith in a woman who has a long record of investigating violence by the state, rather than in a government accused of committing violence and one that has armed and funded it.

And perhaps that is the real measure of the Peace Prize. It cannot compel governments to change course, but it can deny them the final word on their own actions. Thanks to Pillay’s work, the world cannot be prevented from considering the evidence of the destruction of Gaza — however furiously the powerful may object.

The writer is copy editor, The Indian Express. saptarshi.basak@

title: Governor’s rule in KPK: Why Imran Khan’s party-led Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government suspended
text:
Why was governor’s rule imposed?

The federal cabinet recommended the measures under Articles 232 and 234 of Pakistan’s Constitution after reviewing the security situation. The Prime Minister’s Office accused the provincial government of “deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”, Dawn reported.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said civilians, police personnel and security officials had faced repeated attacks, Geo News reported. He also claimed the federal government had provided KP with Rs 800 billion over the past decade to support counterterrorism efforts, but alleged that the provincial government had failed to strengthen its Counter Terrorism Department (CTD), according to the report.

Speaking to Geo News, Prime Minister’s adviser Rana Sanaullah alleged that the provincial government had not endorsed the national position against terrorism. He claimed that five of the 12 districts identified for emergency measures lacked police stations or a CTD presence.

What changes under governor’s rule?

Sharif has formed an 11-member committee, led by Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar, to monitor governance, security and day-to-day affairs in the province, Geo News noted. Representatives of the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), Balochistan Awami Party (BAP) and Istehkam-e-Pakistan Party (IPP) will also be included in the committee, Geo News reported, citing sources.

Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar also said the provincial government had been rendered inactive under the presidential proclamation, as per Geo News. The emergency covers Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, Lakki Marwat, Bannu, Bajaur, Mohmand, Khyber, Kurram, Orakzai, North Waziristan and South Waziristan, with the latter divided administratively into Upper and Lower South Waziristan, according to the report.

PTI’s response and latest developments

PTI chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan said the party would challenge the governor’s rule at every forum. General Secretary Salman Akbar Raja confirmed to Geo News that PTI would approach the courts, arguing that the move undermined the province’s elected mandate.

The decision came a week after the party supporters gathered in the province intending to march towards Islamabad to demand Khan’s release, Reuters said. PTI has maintained that peaceful protest is its constitutional right.

PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari, an aide to Imran Khan, condemned the government’s move to impose an emergency, calling it a “coup disguised as emergency”, according to Reuters. He also reportedly warned that the move could trigger further bloodshed and instability, alleging it was aimed at stopping protests.

Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, who has been engaged by the government to mediate with PTI, also criticised the move, calling the imposition of emergency “an ambush on democracy”, Reuters said.

title: Shekhar Suman did TV to pay for son’s treatment, became highest-paid at Rs 35 cr in 1997
text:
Talking about the tough phase, Shekhar said in a recent interview that he had to take television offers, despite being initially uninterested, because he had no other option. “I discovered my son was terminally ill. Firstly, I had no work at that time. On top of that, we received such tragic news. I was completely ruined and destroyed. I thought I had nothing left in life. I wasn’t earning that much to look after him. I didn’t want to take money from home either. Those were very trying times,” he said, adding that Dekh Bhai Dekh was his first TV show.

Shekhar’s first film deal was for Rs 25,000

Shekhar also admitted in the new interview that Rs 35 crore was a dream for someone who was paid Rs 25,000 for his debut film role in Girish Karnad’s 1984 period drama, Utsav. He claimed even that was “enormous” for him, given prior to that in Delhi, he’d get a salary of Rs 600 for working at the Shri Ram Centre for Performing Arts and his wife Alka Suman would earn Rs 900 per month for working at a shop.

“With Rs 1500, we had a beautiful life. We’d spend Rs 400 on barsati rent, Rs 200 for grocery, Rs 200 for motorcycle petrol, Rs 200 for entertainment, and save whatever was left. The simpler the life is, it’s more beautiful. Then it becomes difficult, particularly for an actor, with ego, fame, money, and jealousy involved. That’s where the person gets trapped, which is not important. The most beautiful thing is you get up in the morning and go to work. People forget your name once you die, but they don’t forget the work you left behind. So, make your work immortal instead of your name,” said Shekhar.

Shekhar Suman was called TV’s Amitabh Bachchan

Shekhar’s TV career took off after Dekh Bhai Dekh. He was hailed as “the Amitabh Bachchan of television” three years before the megastar himself made his small-screen debut as the host of popular quiz show Kaun Banega Crorepati, a role he continues to take on even 26 years and 18 seasons later. While the moniker bothered Shekar initially, he looks back at it with gratitude now.

“Back then, I used to get upset. I had an existence of my own. I wanted to be known as Shekhar Suman. But Amitabh Bachchan is a metaphor. It’s another name for excellence. Being called the ‘Amitabh Bachchan of television’ just means you’re also trying to achieve the same kind of excellence. It’s a very big compliment. I think I was being very stupid,” said Shekhar in a recent interview.

He confessed to The Lallantop that he considers being called TV’s Amitabh Bachchan as prized as the time when then-Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee stopped his cavalcade at a wedding, got down from his car, hugged Shekhar, and asked him to keep satirizing his own personality on his popular late night talk show Movers & Shakers.

title: Apple debuts HomeView, a smart display powered by Siri AI; new HomePod Mini 2 and Apple TV 4k
text:
Siri AI is central to HomeView. It sits at the core of HomeView and draws on personal context from the user’s iPhone. A demo video showed a family using it to find a recipe a parent had texted, check the calendar, and manage a chaotic morning. The examples of everyday use included asking when to leave for a meeting or whether there is a Starbucks at the user’s airport terminal, with the device already aware of the flight details on the user’s phone. Apart from an array of intelligent features, the HomeView also plays music, podcasts and TV. It supports FaceTime calls, shows recipes while users cook, and controls smart home accessories. Apple has also introduced a wall-mounted version with the same display and features, along with an audio experience that is tuned for wall placement.

Apple said that FaceTime is a standout feature on HomeView. The device uses Centre Stage, which pairs an ultra-wide camera with on-device algorithms to track where a person’s torso is. This means if a user is cooking in the kitchen and moving around, the camera pans to keep them in frame. When more people join the call, it widens the shot to fit them. Apple said it put considerable thought into the FaceTime experience so it would work well on a device that stays in one place.

Apple emphasised that privacy is at the core of all its products, and HomeView was designed with privacy in mind. For HomeView specifically, the camera and microphone feeds are secured and processed within exclaves, which are compartmentalised, protected runtimes separate from the operating system. They can’t be accessed by anyone, including Apple. Consequently, to access personal content, a user needs to have been recognised by HomeView, have their iPhone on the same Wi-Fi network, and have recently unlocked it. In case HomeView determines that it cannot recognise a user for any reason, the user will get a confirmation on their phone.

HomeView is compatible with iPhones running on the latest iOS. Both the tabletop and wall-mounted models will be priced at Rs 39,900. Pre-orders will begin on October 13 with availability from November 1 in eight countries: Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, the UK, and the US. The device will ship with English as the primary language for now, but more languages will be added soon.

HomePod Mini 2 with Siri AI

Apple has introduced the new HomePod Mini 2 in blue, green, and pink alongside the existing white and midnight options. A notable addition to the new generation of HomePod Mini is a feature called Sound Glow that makes the light on the top of the speaker glow in colours similar to those of the album art of the song being played. The colours are soft and not meant to pop out, and users also have the option to disable it. Besides, the HomePod Mini 2 can also be connected to a Mac and serve as its audio output for everything from video calls to games. During the demo, Apple showed a HomePod Mini colour-matched to an iMac.
