title: 25, only son: UP sailor among 2 missing after drone attack in Oman
text:
Just a day earlier, Amit had told his family he would be home for Diwali.

“He spoke to his mother, Poonam Devi, on Saturday, telling her he would return home this month to celebrate the festival with us,” said Amit’s uncle, Rajendra Singh, who is also in the Merchant Navy. “We are desperately hoping for good news and his safe return.”

First time at sea

Amit, who is unmarried, went to sea for the first time in January this year after completing a General Purpose (GP) Rating course. He joined the vessel as an Able Seaman.

“He had always wanted to join the merchant navy… like several members of our family who are in the profession,” said Ravindra.

He said that when Preeti told him that Amit’s phone was unreachable, he sent a message but it went undelivered, prompting him to reach out to people in Oman for information.

“I was told that the vessel had been stationed at Sohar Anchorage for several days. On Sunday, all 12 crew members — 11 Indians and one Bangladeshi national — had been called aboard for maintenance work,” he said.

“Later, 10 crew members left the vessel to eat food. Amit and Veer Bahadur stayed back, telling the others that they would join them shortly. Then the drone struck.”

Amit, from Gopalpur village, was unmarried. He was the only son of farmer Dev Prakash Singh and Poonam.

India condemns attacks

Sunday’s incident is the latest in a series of attacks on commercial vessels since the West Asia war broke out.

On Monday, India condemned attacks on two ships with Indians on board in the Strait of Hormuz. “We condemn the attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz region on 11 October 2026. MT PETRO DOLPHIN was reportedly struck by a drone, with two of the 11 Indian seafarers onboard reported missing. MT VALTHERA, a Marshall Islands-flagged tanker, was struck by an unknown projectile, resulting in a fire onboard. All 11 Indian seafarers onboard MT VALTHERA are reported to be safe,” it said.

Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said that tanker MT PETRO DOLPHIN, carrying 11 Indian seafarers, was subjected to a drone attack at Sohar Anchorage. In a social media post on X, Sonowal said that while nine Indian crew members had been successfully rescued and were safe, two Indian nationals remained missing.

He further said search-and-rescue operations were actively underway by the local Coast Guard. “We are continuously coordinating with all relevant authorities to fully support the ongoing rescue efforts and ensure every possible action is taken to safely locate our missing personnel,” Sonowal said.

title: Can makeup beat facial recognition tech? What Richa Chadha’s ‘tutorial’ gets right, and wrong
text:
From submarines to humans: The CV Dazzle project

The idea of using makeup to beat machines is not new.

In 2010, American artist Adam Harvey’s CV Dazzle (Computer Vision Dazzle) project explored how unconventional makeup and hairstyles could interfere with computer vision algorithms.

“Unlike disruptive-pattern material, CV Dazzle is bright and bold, and evades detection by breaking weaknesses in automated pattern recognition systems,” his website says.

Harvey was inspired by the Dazzle initiative used by the British during World War I, when naval ships were painted in high-contrast colours, and patterns such as stripes and geometric, Cubist-like shapes, to confuse enemy observers about their size, shape, direction and speed. Rather than concealing the ships, the designs were intended to make them harder to track and target.

Story continues below this ad

Harvey’s project, developed as part of his master’s thesis at New York University, did see some success, but facial recognition technology has advanced significantly since then.

How does facial recognition work?

Broadly, facial recognition involves matching a face with one stored in the system database.

But facial recognition systems do not simply compare two photographs pixel by pixel. They use artificial intelligence models to analyse a face and convert its visual characteristics into a numerical representation, often called a face embedding. This is compared with representations stored in a database to determine whether there is a likely match.

The system learns patterns associated with identity from training data. Makeup can alter the image presented to the model, potentially changing the numerical representation enough to prevent a match. This does not necessarily stop the system from detecting that a face is present; it may simply fail to establish whose face it is.

Chadha’s method largely depends on drawing extra eyes and lips to confuse machines, and using colour to alter light and dark patterns of a face.

Story continues below this ad

Israeli university’s research on facial recognition

More than a decade after Harvey, in 2021, researchers at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev found that “software-generated makeup patterns can be used to consistently bypass state-of-the-art facial recognition software, with digitally and physically-applied makeup fooling some systems with a success rate as high as 98 percent,” the university’s website says.

The researchers defined their 20 participants as “blacklisted”, so the system would know to look for them. The physical experiment involved two cameras, different shooting angles and varying lighting conditions. The researchers “used a selfie app called YouCam Makeup to digitally apply makeup to the facial images according to the heatmap which targets the most identifiable regions of the face. A makeup artist then emulated the digital makeup onto the participants using natural-looking makeup…” The university says.

title: Lesson from IITs: Excellence is nurtured, not inherited
text:
Advertisement

Universities depend on faculty, students, non-teaching staff and members of governing boards. Strong institutions are serious about whom they bring in and continually seek to raise the quality of their people in all these roles. At leading universities, there is often an implicit aspiration that every new faculty appointment should be at least as good as, and preferably better than, the faculty already there. A mediocre appointment can affect an institution for decades. Recruiting outstanding people is only the beginning. A strong institution should enable talented people to become even better over time, expanding their capabilities and ambition rather than allowing them to stagnate.

Universities also need resources: Buildings, hostels, laboratories, libraries, scholarships and research support. These come not only from government grants or tuition fees; alumni, donors and industry relationships are important institutional assets. A strong university will probably never feel that it has enough resources, because greater ambition creates new possibilities and new needs. It must therefore keep building resources and directing them to the right academic priorities.

This is where governance and culture become crucial. Universities need sufficient autonomy for decisions to be taken close to where information and responsibility reside. They need transparent processes, appropriate delegation and clear accountability. Culture is less visible but equally consequential. When people are respected, information is shared, participation is sought and differing views are genuinely considered, they are more likely to feel ownership of the institution. That ownership brings the ideas, energy and passion of faculty, staff and students into building the university.

The IITs benefited from substantial public investment and, compared to typical Indian universities, had a strong resource base. They attracted highly capable students and were exacting in faculty recruitment, with a strong norm that positions need not be filled if suitable candidates were not found. They also enjoyed considerable academic autonomy, with substantial freedom to shape curricula, teaching, faculty recruitment and internal academic practices. Uniformity in curricula, grading or recruitment practices across the IIT system was not the guiding principle; each institution had room to innovate and develop its own identity. This combination helped the IITs build strong institutions. But they are not permanently protected from decline. If recruitment standards weaken, governance deteriorates, culture erodes or autonomy becomes less purposeful, they too can lose ground.

The three pillars reinforce one another. Institutions with sound governance and a strong culture find it easier to attract good people. title: Work just 3 days a week? Jeff Bezos says AI could change future of work
text:
Bezos also suggested that rising productivity could make two-income households less necessary.

“You’re not going to need to have a two-earner household. If you want it, fine. If you don’t want to have it, one of the people might drop out,” Bezos said. “It’s going to be difficult to hire people, because the productivity in the economy will make it so that [if] people don’t want to work two jobs, they won’t have to.”

His outlook stands in contrast to warnings from other technology leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who have raised concerns about the risks associated with AI.

‘Good thing for society’

Bezos, however, sees the technology as an opportunity to reshape the economy and improve people’s quality of life.

That optimism does not mean he is convinced every company investing in AI will succeed. Asked whether the current AI boom amounts to a bubble, Bezos said it was “hard to know”.

While he believes technology has genuine potential, he acknowledged that the rush to develop and commercialise it has made it difficult to distinguish promising businesses from those unlikely to deliver.

“What I do know is the technology is real. I think this is a good thing for society. It’s tricky for investors. Every experiment gets funded — good ideas and bad ideas. In the moment, in the tussle of this, it’s hard for investors to know the difference between the good ideas and the bad ideas.”

Bezos is not alone in predicting that AI could reduce the amount of time people spend at work.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has suggested that advances in the technology could make a four-day working week possible, and JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has predicted that people might work just three and a half days a week, according to Fortune.

Tesla boss Elon Musk has gone a step further, arguing that improvements in AI and robotics could eventually make employment optional. He has suggested that this shift could happen within the next 10 to 20 years, pointing to a future in which people may no longer need to work to meet their basic needs.

title: Hunter of underwater threats, why INS Mangrol holds importance for the Navy
text:
In total, 16 ASW-SWCs are being constructed together by the CSL and the Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers (GRSE), Kolkata. With over 80% indigenous content, the programme reflects India’s expanding capabilities in naval design, systems integration and defence shipbuilding, the Ministry of Defence has said.

INS Mangrol is named after the coastal town and prominent fishing harbour of Mangrol in Gujarat’s Junagadh district, reflecting the region’s rich maritime heritage. The ship carries forward the legacy of the erstwhile INS Mangrol (M85), a minesweeper that served the Indian Navy from 1983 to 2004.

The crest of INS Mangrol features a Panjmukh, a five-pronged weapon. A social media post about the ship commissioning stated, “Like a Pied Kingfisher, we strike with precision”. The Pied Kingfisher is a striking black-and-white waterbird with a sharply pointed bill and distinctive hovering flight. It is native to the coastal waters of Mangrol.

The features of Mahe class

Built by CSL, the Mahe-class vessels adhere to the classification standards of Det Norske Veritas (DNV), an internationally recognised body that certifies ships against rigorous technical and safety requirements.

They are the Indian Navy’s largest warships to use a diesel engine-waterjet propulsion system, combining improved manoeuvrability with reduced underwater noise. While their primary role is anti-submarine warfare in coastal waters, the vessels are also designed for underwater surveillance, search and rescue (SAR), Low Intensity Maritime Operations (LIMO) and mine-laying. These ships were designed after considering anti-submarine and patrolling operations along the littoral zone.

CSL has stated that each vessel is 78 metres long, has a beam, or maximum width, of 11.36 metres, and a displacement ranging from 896 to 1,100 tonnes. With a maximum speed of 25 knots (about 46 kmph) and the ability to move up to 1,800 nautical miles (approximately 3,333 km) without refuelling, the ships are equipped to operate indigenously developed sonar systems that use sound waves to detect underwater objects.

Their advanced sensors, weapons and communication suites enable the detection, tracking and engagement of underwater threats. The class also features sophisticated machinery, automation and integrated control systems to support sustained operations in shallow waters. Its armament includes torpedoes, multifunctional anti-submarine rockets, and advanced radar and sonar systems.

The need for ships that hunt sub-surface threats

Before the ASW-SWC programme, the Indian Navy relied on four Abhay-class corvettes (which are faster and smaller ships), customised variants of the Soviet-origin Pauk II-class, for coastal patrol and anti-submarine warfare.

After decades of service, these vessels were decommissioned between 2017 and October 2025. To replace the ageing fleet and bolster coastal defence, the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) approved the procurement of 16 ASW-SWCs in December 2

title: WTC Points Table 2025-27: Updated World Test Championship standings after AUS thrash SA in 1st Test
text:
Australia have strengthened their grip at the top of the World Test Championship 2025-27 standings after a dominant performance on the final day in Durban sealed a crushing 214-run win over South Africa, giving the visitors a 1-0 lead in the three-match series.

The Durban Test swung one way and then the other before Australia took complete control, thanks largely to a career-best performance from Player of the Match Matt Renshaw. Reduced to 124/6 on Day 1 by a lively South African seam attack, Renshaw produced a superb rescue act, scoring 190 and sharing an 83-run stand with Pat Cummins and a record 123-run partnership with Nathan Lyon to lift Australia to 390. That gave the tourists a handy 106-run first-innings lead. Renshaw struck again in the second innings, hitting a brisk 82 off 99 balls alongside Nic Maddinson’s 48, helping Australia declare at 314/6. Set an improbable 421 to win, South Africa’s resistance, built around Aiden Markram’s gritty 75, fell apart on the final day against Josh Hazlewood’s relentless spell of 6/49. Renshaw even picked up his maiden Test wicket as the hosts were bowled out for 206.

title: ‘My self-worth depends on career’: Ekta Kapoor lived at office for 6 months, had ‘no life’
text:
Ekta Kapoor recalls mother showering her with flowers

Ekta recalled calling her mother one day to say that she would be coming home at 11 pm to sleep. Her mother was so surprised by the announcement that Ekta jokingly asked her to shower her with flowers when she arrived.

“When I finally came home, my mother showered me with flowers because I hadn’t been home for six months, except to take a shower. My house was just 10 minutes away from my office,” she recalled.

Ekta said although her home was just 10 minutes away from her office, she continued staying at the office to oversee production.

Story continues below this ad

“My house is just 10 minutes away from my office. I would stay at the office, go upstairs to watch an edit whenever it was ready, come back downstairs to sleep, and then go up again after sleeping for two hours.”

Ekta Kapoor on hustle culture

Ekta also addressed the growing conversation around hustle culture and the idea that working excessively long hours should not be treated as the norm.

“I think people are increasingly saying that we shouldn’t normalise hustle culture, and I hear this more and more. But I think it is a choice. This was my choice. I respect people who don’t want to work this way, and I respect their choices too,” she said.

Story continues below this ad

Ekta described working relentlessly something that gave her personal satisfaction, explaining that she often felt compelled to translate her thoughts and emotions into creative work.

“It was my way of releasing everything I was feeling. I experienced so many things in my life, and until I put them down on paper and created something out of them, I didn’t feel satisfied,” she said.

The producer also spoke about how closely her sense of self-worth is tied to her professional achievements.

“My self-worth comes from my career. It is both a good and a bad thing. The good part is that it helped me create a lot of content, but the bad part is that it is unhealthy,” she said.

Ekta’s daily routine after becoming a mother

Earlier this year on a podcast by Usha Kakade Productions, Ekta had discussed how she manages work alongside motherhood.

Describing her daily routine, Ekta explained that she briefly wakes up when her son gets ready for school before returning to sleep. She then begins her workday late in the morning.

“In the morning when my son goes to school, I wake up for about ten minutes for him and then go back to sleep. I wake up again at around 11 am and spend the next three hours on calls, mobile work and writing content,” she explained.

text:
File photo: US Vice President JD Vance (Picture credit: Reuters)

US Vice President JD Vance has acknowledged that his rhetoric was “imperfect” after describing foreign professionals working on H-1B visas as “indentured servants”, clarifying that his criticism was directed at American companies and the visa system rather than the workers themselves. Speaking at a CBS News town hall on Saturday, Vance said he took responsibility for his choice of words following criticism, including from India, which had described the terminology as “deeply offensive” and said it carried painful historical and colonial legacy connotations. “I would say, and to the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that's on me,” Vance said in response to a question from an Indian immigrant who became a US citizen five years ago and voted for President Donald Trump. Vance argued that the H-1B visa system could leave foreign employees vulnerable because their legal status in the United States is closely tied to their employment. He said employers could exercise excessive control over workers who risk losing their ability to remain in the country if they lose their jobs. The Vice President said his comments were "not a criticism of the H-1B holder." He explained that companies sponsoring H-1B workers certify that they cannot find an alternative American applicant for the position, while the workers’ visas often serve as their “only lifeline to the United States of America”. “So, when I say indentured servitude, that is not a criticism of H1B visa holders; that is the criticism of the company, which brings a person who sometimes will lay off an American worker and knows that if they complain, if they have disagreement with the boss, they could just lose their job… They can be shipped back, which I think gives way too much power to the employer. Maybe my rhetoric has been imperfect here… it is the criticism of the visa system that allowed people to be treated as indentured servants, as they can be shipped to their countries of origin,” Vance added.

Vance says he does not intend to dehumanise immigrants

Vance also referred to his own family while explaining his position on immigration, saying the United States needed to balance welcoming foreign professionals with protecting American workers. “You know where my family comes from, and I love my mother-in-law and father-in-law who immigrated from South India, and obviously their daughter, born in the United States of America, is now the second lady, and I’m very proud of her, and I love her very much,” he said. His wife, Usha Vance, is the daughter of Indian immigrants. Acknowledging that he was not perfect, the Vice President said his intention was not to dehumanise people who had moved to the United States. “I will tell you that nobody's perfect, certainly not me. But my goal here is not to dehumanise any immigrant, and in fact, I love a number of immigrants,” he said.

title: 'Unacceptable': Paswan defends 'Leave India' notice to Imran Khan over Mumbai stir
text:
Union minister Chirag Paswan

NEW DELHI: Union minister Chirag Paswan on Sunday reacted to the ‘Leave India’ notice issued to actor Imran Khan over his participation in protests seeking the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Paswan termed the involvement of foreign nationals in India’s internal affairs “unacceptable”, while expressing support for peaceful protests by Indian citizens. Paswan told news agency ANI that he supported peaceful demonstrations by Indian citizens but questioned the participation of those who do not hold Indian citizenship. “There is no objection to Indian citizens playing a role in matters concerning India while living within the country. I have always supported peaceful protests. However, I do not consider it justifiable for someone who is not an Indian citizen to intervene in India's internal affairs or play a role in such matters,” he said. “For someone who is not an Indian citizen to involve themselves in India's internal affairs—especially when there are growing concerns that foreign forces may be involved in orchestrating these events—is unacceptable,” the Union Minister added. Paswan’s remarks follow the issuance of a ‘Leave India’ notice to Imran Khan by Mumbai Police on Thursday. The notice directs the actor to leave India by October 28. According to ANI, Khan, the nephew of actor Aamir Khan, holds an American passport. Authorities have initiated action against him under Sections 29 and 7 of the Immigration Act over allegations that he participated in a protest despite not being an Indian citizen. Khan had joined a demonstration at Mumbai’s August Kranti Maidan, where protesters demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. He was detained by Mumbai Police last week. After his detention, the actor posted a picture of himself apparently sitting inside a police van, with the caption, “Apparently I’m going for a drive.”

title: France's 140 year old Town Hall survived World Wars but succumbed to protesters
text:
Limoges town hall, a 143-year-old landmark, gutted in fire during violent protests in France

A 143-year-old town hall in the French city of Limoges, which served as a hub for resistance activities during Nazi occupation and hosted Belgium’s government-in-exile in 1940, has been largely destroyed after protesters set it ablaze during violent demonstrations over the cost of living, school conditions and public services. Local officials said around two-thirds of the historic building had been destroyed in the fire, describing the damage as a “catastrophe for heritage”. The destruction came as protests swept across France on Saturday, with demonstrations over rising fuel prices, inflation and deteriorating public services turning violent in several cities. An estimated 550,000 people took part in the marches, according to the French interior ministry.Also Read | Student grievances, cost-of-living crisis, political discontent: Why are protests turning violent in France Dozens of shops were looted in cities including Paris, Marseille, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux, Limoges, Lille, Toulouse and Strasbourg. Fires burned in Paris late into the evening, while riot police used tear gas and baton charges to disperse crowds. The damage to Limoges town hall has put the spotlight on a building with a significant place in the city's wartime history. In May 1940, as Nazi Germany advanced across Europe, Belgian ministers and parliamentarians who had fled their country arrived in Limoges on May 31. They had briefly taken refuge in Poitiers before moving to Limoges, where they were welcomed by the city's then mayor, Léon Betoulle.Also Read | France protests leave Paris streets buried in rubbish amidst violence, looting across nation The Belgian representatives condemned King Leopold III's decision to surrender to the Nazi threat and established their offices in the town hall and the prefecture. Belgian flags were flown alongside French ones, turning the municipal building into a centre of activity for the government-in-exile. During the German occupation of France, the town hall also became an important base for the Resistance in the southern unoccupied zone. Lucien Berdasé, who worked in the municipal administration, helped resistance fighters by sabotaging lists of Jewish residents, preparing false documents and concealing weapons stored in the building. He also arranged travel permits for vehicles used by the *Maquis*, the French resistance fighters. Suzanne Rodi-Boyer, who was responsible for distributing food ration cards at the town hall, helped Jewish families obtain false papers using stamps taken from the municipality. These efforts made the building part of a wider network that helped people evade Nazi persecution and supported resistance activities. The town hall's post-war history included a visit by General Charles de Gaulle on March 4, 1945. Georges Guingouin, a prominent Resistance figure and member of the Order of Liberation, later served as Limoges mayor

title: 'Could not prevent regime change within own party': CM Fadnavis mocks Uddhav
text:
Fadnavis hits back at Uddhav

NEW DELHI: Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis on Sunday hit back at former chief minister Uddhav Thackeray for backing calls for a “regime change” in India, saying the Shiv Sena (UBT) president had failed to prevent a regime change within his own party.Also Read | ‘Taking away right to vote, protest’: Uddhav backs opposition's ‘regime change’ call against government “First of all, Uddhav Thackeray could not prevent a regime change within his own Shiv Sena, so I do not know what other regime change he is talking about. The moment his party abandoned Hindutva and the ideology of Hindu Hriday Samrat Balasaheb Thackeray, such turmoil erupted within the party that those who wanted to follow Balasaheb Thackeray’s principles formed the real Shiv Sena,” Fadnavis told reporters in Nagpur. Fadnavis was referring to the June 2022 split in the undivided Shiv Sena, which led to the formation of two factions led by Uddhav Thackeray and Maharashtra deputy chief Minister Eknath Shinde. The chief minister asserted that any regime change in India could take place only through elections, not through street protests. “I have made it very clear: Stop fighting against the Constitution of India. Decisions in this country will be taken in Parliament and in accordance with the Constitution, not on the streets. In a democracy, governments are decided through elections,” he said. Fadnavis expressed confidence that Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government would return to power in 2029 and called on the opposition to win public support to secure an electoral victory. “Today, Narendra Modi’s government is in power, and it will be elected again. But if you want a regime change, you must contest elections, win the hearts of the people and secure an electoral victory. Those who dream of bringing about a regime change in India by disregarding the Constitution, as witnessed in Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Pakistan, will never succeed in their intentions,” the chief minister added, referring to the youth- and student-led movements that toppled incumbent governments in three of India’s neighbouring countries in recent years. Fadnavis’ comments came a day after Uddhav Thackeray backed recent calls by activists and opposition leaders for a regime change in India, arguing that denying people the right to express their views through elections and protests would leave them with no option but to seek a change of government. “If you take away our right to express our views through elections and protest, then we're standing up just to overthrow this government,” the Shiv Sena (UBT) chief said. The remarks come amid a political row over references to regime change by opposition leaders and student activists during ongoing protests in Delhi against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

title: Gwalior temple tragedy: CM Yadav orders City SP’s removal, 8 others after 14 deaths
text:
MP CM orders removal of CSP, suspension of 8 police personnel over alleged negligence (Photo: ANI).

NEW DELHI: Madhya Pradesh chief minister Mohan Yadav on Sunday ordered the removal of Gwalior’s City SP and eight others over alleged negligence that left 14 dead and 28 injured as a truck rammed into the devotees in a temple. “Instructions have been issued to immediately remove the CSP from his post and suspend three station house officers, one traffic inspector, one head constable, and three constables,” Yadav said in a post on X. Around 1.30 am on Sunday, a truck, with a Punjab registration number, entered the prohibited zone near a slope on Chinor Road and ran over devotees outside the Sheetla Mata temple, in Gwalior district, eventually ramming into its entrance gate. 14 people were killed in the incident; 28 were injured, with seven in critical condition, officials said, as per PTI. Two police personnel were also among the injured. A wall of the temple reportedly collapsed under the impact of the collision. The impact caused a temple wall to collapse, trapping people beneath the debris. The bodies of the deceased and the injured were taken to various hospitals, including the trauma centre in Gwalior. "The accident occurred because the truck entered a prohibited area," Yadav told reporters in Indore, PTI reported. The CM also ordered a detailed investigation into the incident to find those responsible and ensure strict action against the guilty.

title: Google cofounder Sergey Brin donated $100 mn but cannot cast a vote next month
text:
Google cofounder Sergey Brin has emerged as the biggest financial opponent of California’s proposed billionaire wealth tax, contributing more than $100 million to campaigns against the measure. However, the tech billionaire will not be eligible to vote on the proposal next month after changing his voter registration from California to Nevada, according to a Forbes report. Brin has channelled his opposition to the tax through his Build a Better California PAC, making him the largest donor fighting the initiative. The irony, Forbes noted, is that Brin himself will not get a say at the ballot box because public records from the Nevada Secretary of State's office show he changed his voter registration to Nevada on December 10.

Sergey Brin’s move to Nevada linked to tax concerns

According to Forbes, Brin's relocation appears to be part of a broader effort to avoid the proposed tax, which would apply only to California residents as of January 1, 2026. The billionaire purchased a $42 million mansion on the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe in December, and his representatives told Forbes that he is now a Nevada resident. The move also makes Brin, whose net worth is estimated at $263 billion, the richest resident of Nevada, surpassing casino heiress and Republican donor Miriam Adelson, whose fortune is estimated at $31.2 billion. Brin's voter registration reportedly lists his political affiliation as nonpartisan.

What is California's Proposition 40

Proposition 40 will be on the ballot in November. It would impose a one-time 5% tax on California’s 200 billionaires. Ninety percent of the revenue would go to the state’s health care program. The remaining 10% would go to education, food assistance and administration. With a net worth of nearly $260 billion, Brin could owe about $13 billion if it passes.

Billionaires and Gavin Newsom line up against it

Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt and PayPal cofounder Peter Thiel have also donated to groups opposing the measure. Brin has likened the proposal to the socialist society he left behind. “I fled socialism with my family in 1979,” he told The New York Times in April, adding that he does not want California to end up in the same place. Gov. Gavin Newsom has also come out against the tax. He argues it would erode the state’s tax base and cut revenue for social services. In an interview with Bloomberg Businessweek earlier this year, he said it would reduce investment in education, teachers, librarians, childcare, firefighting and police.

Larry Page also shifts residency

Forbes reported that Brin's Google cofounder Larry Page has likewise moved away from California, although he is not yet registered to vote in Florida, according to records reviewed by the publication. Page's representatives told Forbes that his residency has changed from California to Florida. title: ‘With help of God & your prayers’: Pope makes first public appearance after surgery
text:
Pope Leo XIV appears at the window of his study in the Apostolic Palace overlooking St. Peter's Square at the Vatican, a day after he returned from the hospital, where he had lung cancer removed

Pope Leo XIV made his first public appearance on Sunday since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago, addressing crowds gathered in St Peter’s Square from a window of the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace and assuring the faithful that he would gradually return to his duties. The 71-year-old pontiff appeared unaided at the window and delivered his customary Sunday noon address in a firm, clear voice, smiling as he spoke to pilgrims gathered below under cloudy skies. Thanking people around the world for their prayers and support, Leo said he had come through a delicate phase of his recovery and would begin resuming his activities with their continued prayers and God’s help. “Having overcome this delicate phase ... I will now gradually resume my activities, always with the help of God and your prayers,” he said. He also urged pilgrims to put aside selfish ambitions and serve God “without compromise”. The appearance marked Leo’s first public engagement since he underwent an operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung. The surgery, which came during the 71-year-old’s 17-month papacy, had raised questions about how his health might affect his ability to carry out his responsibilities as head of the Catholic Church, which has around 1.4 billion members.

Pope discharged from hospital ahead of schedule

Catholic faithful gathered in St Peter’s Square to welcome Leo back after he was discharged from Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Saturday, four days after the operation. The pontiff had indicated that he was recovering well, telling a reporter in English that he was doing “much better” as he left the hospital. His discharge came earlier than the week-long hospital stay initially anticipated, AP reported. The operation confirmed that Leo had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Tests on the tumour and related lymph nodes were underway, with the results expected to help doctors determine whether he would need further treatment. Possible treatment options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy depending on the tumour’s genetic characteristics, according to news agency AP.

Next major engagement is planned for November

Leo’s next major engagement is an overseas trip scheduled for November 6-17, covering Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. The itinerary includes a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high-altitude locations. His surgeon, Dr Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that there were “no clinical reasons” to rule out the trip. Margaritora said the pontiff had devoted considerable effort to his recovery and was expected to recover fully from the operation in around 10 more days. title: Four students build wallet-sized CPR patch with live guidance, win $10,000 prize
text:
The patch uses LED lights to guide chest compressions during CPR. (AI photo)

Performing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) during an emergency can be difficult for someone without proper training. Even when a bystander is willing to help, getting the depth and speed of chest compressions right can be challenging. Four University of Washington students have developed a wallet-sized device that provides visual guidance during CPR. Their invention, called CPRight, won the $10,000 undergraduate first prize at the 2026 Collegiate Inventors Competition, announced on Friday. According to National Inventors Hall of Fame's (NIHF), the device is a small, single-use patch that uses LED lights to indicate whether chest compressions are being performed effectively. Unlike systems that depend on external equipment, CPRight works independently, allowing rescuers to receive feedback while performing CPR. Shubham Bansal, Prisha Hemani, Deeya Sharma and Nikhita Vaddineni developed the invention under the guidance of Tristan Jafari. Their work was recognised at a national competition organised by the National Inventors Hall of Fame (NIHF), which rewards inventions created by university students. The invention addresses a serious problem in emergency medical care. According to the NIHF, more than 350,000 Americans experience out-of-hospital cardiac emergencies annually, with approximately 90% dying. The figures cited by the organisation highlight the importance of effective emergency assistance, particularly when medical professionals are not immediately available.

How the patch helps someone performing CPR

The idea behind CPRight is to give rescuers immediate information about their chest compressions without requiring them to operate another device. Before starting compressions, the rescuer places the patch on the patient's sternum, commonly known as the breastbone. As CPR is performed, its LED indicators show whether the depth and rate of compressions are effective. The patch does not need to be connected to a smartphone or monitoring system. This allows the person performing CPR to receive visual guidance directly from the device. The students have also kept the design compact. Its wallet-sized form and single-use design are intended to make it a practical option for emergency situations. CPRight was one of several medical inventions recognised at this year's competition. While the University of Washington team focused on emergency resuscitation, other student groups worked on problems involving cancer treatment, rehabilitation, shoulder injuries and neurological monitoring.

From knee recovery to monitoring brain activity

One of the other recognised inventions aims to help people recovering from knee injuries or surgery. Rehabilitation can continue for months, and patients may need to perform exercises at home between appointments. title: Vance blames immigration for France unrest as fire guts 143-year-old town hall
text:
US Vice President JD Vance

US Vice President JD Vance has launched a scathing attack on France’s immigration policies, blaming them for the country’s escalating unrest as violent protests over education cuts, rising living costs and public services swept several cities. The demonstrations were marked by arson, looting and clashes with police, with a fire partially destroying the 143-year-old town hall in Limoges. Vance’s remarks follow an earlier intervention by US president Donald Trump, who also attributed the unrest to 'mass migration' and 'Islam', dismissing the protests’ stated concerns over school conditions. In a post on social media, Vance criticised Western governments’ approach to immigration, diversity and assimilation. “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility. They were told it would lead to this and they didn't listen,” Vance said. “I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn. And I hope Americans are paying attention. This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country,” he added. Earlier, in a post on Truth Social, Trump had said, “What's happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration.” “This isn't about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!” Trump added. The protests, which began in late September, initially centred on deteriorating school conditions, teacher shortages and education spending cuts before widening into demonstrations against rising living costs, inequality and pressure on public services. Violence escalated on Saturday, with public buildings and businesses targeted in several cities. In Limoges, the historic town hall was partially destroyed in an arson attack, while Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave said up to 100 shops had been looted. French interior minister Laurent Nuñez said 110 demonstrations had drawn around 5,50,000 people nationwide, including 1,10,000 in Paris. Organisers, including the CGT labour union and student organisations, estimated the turnout at approximately 8,00,000. Nuñez blamed the violence on “extremely violent, radical far-left groups”, alleging that they targeted public buildings and sought confrontations with police. French president Emmanuel Macron condemned the destruction in a post on X, saying, “No room for violence in our Republic. Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished.” French prime minister Sébastien Lecornu also said the government would not be intimidated by violence, distinguishing peaceful demonstrations from arson, looting and attacks on property.

End of Article

title: 'Samson plays with emotions': Why Sooryavanshi will have to wait for his chance
text:
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and Sanju Samson

Former India assistant coach Abhishek Nayar believes Sanju Samson’s ability to bounce back with a big innings after a few low scores could mean Vaibhav Sooryavanshi will have to wait for his chance in the upcoming T20I series against New Zealand. Nayar also explained how India’s team combination, particularly the need for a left-right batting pair, could influence the selection decision. Samson’s inconsistent performances have often raised questions about his place in India’s T20I side, with Sooryavanshi seen as a possible replacement. However, Nayar believes Samson’s ability to respond to criticism with a big score makes it difficult for the team management to move on from him. “Sanju plays with everyone’s emotions because he won’t score runs for two matches, and everyone starts raising questions, ‘Vaibhav Sooryavanshi should play, Sanju Samson isn’t capitalising on his chances, how long will we wait?’ And at that very moment, he will score an 80 in no time. Sanju is that kind of player who will repeatedly give you opportunities to raise questions about him and then will play a big knock, making the most of his chances. So, there will be moments when there will be talks about his place, but Vaibhav Sooryavanshi will have to wait,” Nayar told JioStar, as quoted by news agency IANS. Nayar said the selection call would depend on more than just individual performances. He stressed that team balance and the management’s approach to selection were also important, warning that frequent changes could affect the team's culture and the development of young players.

title: Barbra Streisand’s $10m gift backs women’s heart center leading $7.5m aging study
text:
Women’s health research is shifting towards a whole-body approach, connecting heart, brain, mobility and ageing to improve long-term wellbeing.

Aging is rarely a single-system story. The heart, brain, muscles and blood vessels change together, yet medical research has often studied them separately. A new five-year research project at Cedars-Sinai is taking a broader view, investigating whether damage to the body’s smallest blood vessels could help explain several health challenges women face as they grow older. Backed by a $7.5 million grant from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the National Institute on Aging (NIA), the study brings together specialists in cardiovascular health, neurology, biostatistics and frailty research. At its centre is a question with implications far beyond cardiology: could understanding tiny blood vessels reveal new ways to protect the ageing heart, brain and body?

Looking beyond the heart

The research is being led by investigators at the Smidt Heart Institute’s Barbra Streisand Women’s Heart Center, named after the legendary singer and actor following her $10 million donation to Cedars-Sinai. The new initiative, known as the Microvascular Aging Effects—Women’s Evaluation of Systemic Aging Tenacity in Heart, Brain and Frailty study, or MAE-WEST HBF, has been established as a Specialized Center of Research Excellence on Sex Differences through the NIH Office of Research on Women’s Health. Its focus is the microvasculature: the network of tiny blood vessels that delivers oxygen and nutrients throughout the body. Researchers want to understand how deterioration in these vessels may connect not only to cardiovascular disease but also to cognitive decline and reduced physical strength.

A trail of clues

The project builds on years of work at Cedars-Sinai examining coronary microvascular disease, a condition that affects the smallest blood vessels supplying the heart and is more common in women. Previous research from the Barbra Streisand Women’s Heart Center has linked small-vessel disease, chronic inflammation and iron accumulation with impaired function in the heart, brain and kidneys, alongside declining physical strength. That history gives the new study a strong foundation. Rather than examining individual conditions in isolation, researchers will explore whether they share underlying biological pathways. The distinction is important because women can experience cardiovascular symptoms that are less obvious than the classic signs associated with heart disease. Microvascular disease has historically been overlooked or mistaken for other conditions, leaving some patients without appropriate diagnosis or treatment.

title: Utah couple builds $2m backyard scuba pool with 90-foot mountain and lazy river
text:
Photo: Crazy World

A Utah couple wanted a place where they could practise scuba diving without travelling to the ocean. Their solution was to build a $2 million backyard swimming pool with 360,000 gallons of water, a 90-foot man-made mountain, five waterfalls and an underwater tunnel that takes divers down to a depth of 26 feet. Called “The Mountain”, the pool was built at a home in Springville, Utah. It stretches 140 feet long and 60 feet wide, and includes a 300-foot lazy river, a hidden grotto, winding pathways and a water slide concealed inside the mountain. As reported by FOX 13 News, the unusual pool was featured on Animal Planet’s television programme ‘The Pool Master,’ hosted by pool designer Anthony Archer-Wills. The project was designed for a homeowner who loved mountains and scuba diving, the broadcaster reported.

A 90-foot mountain in the backyard

The pool’s main feature is a 90-foot artificial mountain designed to resemble the natural landscape around the property. It includes five waterfalls, several hidden pathways and two bridges that wind towards the top. Archer-Wills described the structure as one that “emulates the natural surroundings perfectly”, according to FOX 13 News. The mountain is not just decorative. A hidden water slide runs for 60 feet through the structure before dropping into the pool below. There is also a secluded grotto tucked behind the waterfalls, giving swimmers another place to explore. The pool’s design combines these features with a 300-foot lazy river, allowing the owners to swim, float and explore different parts of the property without leaving home.

A tunnel that lets the owners practise scuba diving

Photo: Crazy World

Scuba diving was one of the main reasons the couple commissioned the pool. Utah is far from the ocean, so having a deep-water area at home offered them a place to practise. According to FOX 13 News, a concealed entrance inside the mountain leads to a tunnel measuring 54 feet long and five feet wide. The tunnel reaches a depth of 26 feet and connects to the main pool. The underwater section is intended for scuba-certified divers. It allows them to put on diving equipment and practise underwater skills without travelling to a coastal diving location. As reported by Scuba Diving magazine, the $2 million project included the 54-foot tunnel, five waterfalls, the lazy river and a hidden 60-foot slide in the year 2014.

A kitchen, bridges and hidden spaces

The pool also has facilities for spending time outdoors beyond swimming and diving. According to FOX 13 News, the mountain houses a full kitchen with granite countertops, stainless-steel cabinets, a refrigerator and an eight-burner grill. The bridges and paths offer access to the upper sections of the structure, while the hidden grotto and winding passages give the mountain several enclosed spaces to explore. title: America's biggest investor, who predicted the 2008 crash, shares 10 life lessons
text:
America’s biggest investor Michael Burry, who predicted the popular US housing crash of 2008 has shared a concise list of life lessons covering everything from personal finance and relationships to parenting and charity. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Burry posted a 10-point guide that combines investment principles with broader advice on living a fulfilling life. Topping the list, Burry urged people to continuously improve themselves, writing: "Never stop exercising or learning." Burry also talked about the importance of compounding, a concept which is associated with investing. "Manifest the power of compounding," Burry said, suggesting that small, consistent efforts can generate significant long-term benefits.

Advice on relationships and family

Apart from money and investing, Burry also highlighted the value of personal relationships and family. He has also asked the users to "accept compromise to begin relationships," underscoring the role of flexibility in building meaningful connections. He encouraged the people to have children and be responsible parents, writing: "Have kids and be a good parent."

Avoid unnecessary financial risks

Several of Burry's points focused on financial discipline. He warned against gambling, stating simply: "Never gamble." He also offered a housing tip that reflects a conservative approach to personal finance: "Buy half the house you can afford." Another recommendation was, "If it flies or floats, rent it," a reference to expensive assets such as aircraft and boats that can be costly to own and maintain.

Be grateful and give back

Burry's final pieces of advice centred on gratitude and generosity. "Be thankful for and to all," he wrote, before concluding his list with: "Be charitable." He also touched on art and spending habits, stating: "Art in the eye of the beholder is cheap," suggesting that personal appreciation matters more than price tags. title: New Jersey court upholds will cutting two sons out of mother’s estate
text:
A New Jersey mother removed both sons from her will in 2016 after their relationship deteriorated. (AI image)

A New Jersey mother who once planned to leave her property equally to her four children later decided that her two sons would receive nothing. She made the change in 2016, following a breakdown in their relationship, while one of her daughters had been caring for her for years. After the woman died in 2024, the sons challenged her decision in court, claiming their sisters had influenced her. However, on Friday, a New Jersey appeals court upheld the revised will, finding insufficient evidence that the mother had been pressured into changing it. According to details of the case published by Law.com, the woman signed the will in 1996. At the time, she wanted her estate divided equally among her two sons and two daughters. She also chose one son and one daughter to handle her affairs after her death jointly. That same year, her daughter Deborah became her sole caregiver and began living in the family home. Over the following years, Deborah continued looking after her mother, while relations between the woman and her sons eventually deteriorated. The situation changed in 2015 after a family altercation. The mother's relationship with her sons became strained, and in some periods, they reportedly had no contact. A year later, she signed another will that excluded both sons, and Deborah was also named the sole person responsible for handling the estate after her mother's death.

A family rift, a new will and a legal challenge

The disagreement over this decision did not reach court immediately. The mother continued living for another eight years, during which questions were raised about whether someone close to her was taking advantage of her financially. In 2021, New Jersey's Adult Protective Services Programme investigated a complaint alleging financial exploitation. The investigation did not find evidence to substantiate the allegation, and the matter was closed. When the mother died in 2024, one of her sons objected to the revised will. Both sons subsequently challenged the arrangements, questioning whether their mother had made the decision independently. Their argument focused largely on the relationships she shared with her daughters. Deborah had been her caregiver since 1996, and the mother was also close to her other daughter. The sons believed these circumstances raised doubts about whether she had acted entirely of her own choice.

Sons believe their mother was influenced

The sons argued that their mother's dependence on Deborah for care, together with her close relationship with their other sister, should have prompted greater scrutiny of the 2016 will. They wanted the court to require their sisters to demonstrate that their mother had not been improperly influenced The daughters rejected these claims. title: FMCG firms feel the pinch: Will your favourite products cost more this Diwali?
text:
FMCG price hikes may follow after Diwali as costs climb

The festive season may bring cheer to shoppers, but for FMCG companies, rising costs are turning out to be a bitter pill. With prices of key raw materials climbing, companies are struggling to protect their profit margins without making everyday products more expensive for consumers. The big question now is whether they can keep prices in check for much longer, especially in price-sensitive mass-market and rural segments. The pressure has increased in the September quarter, reversing some of the relief companies saw in the previous quarter. Firms absorbed part of the cost increase to keep products affordable during the festive season, but this has squeezed their margins. The rise in costs has not been the same across all commodities. Crude oil-linked materials, packaging, palm oil and sugar have emerged as major pressure points, said Naveen Malpani, Partner and Consumer Industry Leader at Grant Thornton Bharat. "In rupee terms, palm oil prices were approximately 21 per cent higher year-on-year in September, while sugar prices remained around 18 per cent higher year-on-year despite correcting 8 per cent month-on-month," he said. Companies have not been able to make up for the higher costs through price increases and efficiency improvements alone, putting pressure on their operating margins, Malpani said. "Pre-results analyst estimates projected operating-margin compression of approximately 45 basis points year-on-year across a group of major consumer staples companies, with some estimates indicating declines of up to 150 basis points for the companies covered," he said. For companies selling everyday products to mass-market consumers, raising prices sharply is not an easy option. Higher prices could make products less affordable, leaving companies to rely on cost-cutting, better procurement and carefully planned price changes to protect profits without hurting demand. “The sector should therefore prepare for continued margin pressure through H2, with recovery contingent on actual commodity movements rather than an assumption that the cost cycle has peaked,” Malpani added.

Price hikes may have to wait until after the festive season

For now, FMCG companies are trying to absorb some of the cost shock rather than pass it all on to consumers. Parle Products Chief Marketing Officer Mayank Shah told PTI that rising inflation was a major concern for the FMCG industry and was “definitely worrisome”. However, companies are attempting to cushion the impact on their margins by improving efficiency and cutting costs instead of immediately increasing prices, he said. Demand remains robust across urban and rural India, Shah said, adding that companies had avoided passing on the entire increase in input costs to consumers. That could change after the festive season. Companies may consider raising prices depending on how agricultural commodity prices move and how the broader geopolitical situation unfolds.

title: Woman locks herself in room with 2 children, attacks them with scissors; all 3 die
text:
Usha took the children into a room and locked the door before attacking them with scissors. She then allegedly inflicted injuries on herself, police said.

JAIPUR: A woman allegedly killed her two minor children with scissors before dying by suicide in Rajasthan’s Alwar district on Sunday, police said. The incident took place in Dantiya village near Kherli town, where Usha Sharma allegedly attacked her five-year-old son, Mukul, and four-year-old daughter, Nandini, following an argument over the girl going outside to play, police said. Usha took the children into a room and locked the door before attacking them with scissors. She then allegedly inflicted injuries on herself, police said. According to news agency PTI, villagers rushed to the house after hearing the children scream and forced open the door, where they found the woman and her two children lying injured. Usha's younger sister Manisha, who was present at the house, became distressed on seeing them and injured herself by banging her head against a wall and the floor. Villagers rushed all four to the sub-district hospital in Kherli, where doctors declared Mukul dead. Usha and Nandini died during treatment. Manisha, who sustained serious injuries, was referred to a district hospital for further treatment. Police said Usha’s husband, Amit Sharma, works for a private company in Gujarat, while Manisha’s husband, Ankit Sharma, works as a nurse at a private hospital in Jaipur. Kathumar circle officer Joginder Singh Rajawat and Kherli police reached the village and inspected the scene. The bodies have been kept in the mortuary of the Kherli hospital. Further investigation is underway.(With agency inputs)

End of Article

title: Why should MEA question CM role on foreign trip: HC
text:
Punjab’s govt had moved HC after the MEA “denied” its plea for clearance without assigning any reason

CHANDIGARH: The Punjab and Haryana high court has observed that the MEA had “not explained” the political angle it cited while turning down political clearance to Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann for his visit to France. The court released the detailed order on Saturday, a day after it allowed Punjab govt’s plea to let Mann fly to France for SIAL Paris 2026, a food and beverage innovation trade fair to be attended by the state-run Markfed. The ministry of external affairs (MEA) had refused to let Mann visit France, citing a “political angle”. In its detailed order, the court said: “It has not been explained what that political angle/viewpoint is, and whether political clearance means examining the application from a political angle. No reasons are forthcoming.” Justice Tribhuvan Dahiya rejected Centre’s justification that there was no proper invitation from the French govt and the CM had no functional role to perform during the proposed visit. The bench held that the reasons subsequently offered in an affidavit could not be used to justify the original decision. The HC allowed the petition filed by the Punjab govt challenging the denial of political clearance to a three-member delegation comprising the CM, the chief secretary and the principal secretary to the CM for a visit to Paris from Oct 17 to 21 to promote trade and attend the SIAL food exhibition. The court observed that the contention regarding the absence of a proper invitation from the foreign govt “cannot be accepted” in view of a Sept 22 letter sent by SIAL to the French Embassy in India. The letter stated, “We are very pleased to count among our visitors Mr. Bhagwant Mann ... (w)e are convinced that this is an opportunity for Mr. Bhagwant Mann to establish professional contacts with French and international visitors and to negotiate contracts. ” Rejecting the second justification that the CM had no functional role during the visit, the bench observed that it cannot be accepted as “he himself is heading the delegation”. The bench questioned the requirement for the ministry to examine the CM’s functional role during the visit. “Further, it has not been explained as to why is there a requirement for the ministry to examine functional role of the chief minister during the proposed visit,” it observed. “The requirement appears to be superfluous for the reason the clearance has been denied due to ‘political angle’ alone, and not on any functional aspect of the dignitary’s visit,” the bench added. The high court also relied on the Supreme Court Constitution Bench judgment in Mohinder Singh Gill and another versus The Chief Election Commissioner, New Delhi and others, 1978 AIR Supreme Court 851, to emphasise that the “validity of an order must be judged by the reasons mentioned therein which cannot be supplemented by fresh reasons in the shape of an affidavit or otherwise”. “Accordingly,

title: 'You are ruining entire town': With pistol in hand, B'desh minister raids drug den; watch
text:
Bangladesh minister Ishraque Hossain raids a suspected drug den in Dhaka with a pistol in hand, sparking debate on social media

A Bangladeshi minister triggered a debate on social media after carrying out a raid on a suspected drug den in a Dhaka slum on Saturday, armed with a pistol and accompanied by associates, at least one of whom was also seen carrying a handgun. State minister for liberation war affairs Ishraque Hossain shared a video of the raid, showing him stepping out of a vehicle with a megaphone in one hand and a pistol in the other before chasing a group of people near Gandaria Railway Station. “You are ruining the entire town, destroying the entire area,” Hossain, 39, was heard telling the group in the footage, news agency PTI reported. Some of the men detained by his associates claimed they were innocent. “Let police come, then there will be talks,” Hossain was heard responding. Police said the minister had not informed them about the raid beforehand. He and his associates detained six people and handed them over to the local police station, according to officials. "The minister did not inform us about the raid in advance; we learned about it afterwards,” Dhaka metropolitan police’s additional deputy commissioner Masud Rana told reporters. Hossain, a member of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), was elected to Parliament from the area in the February 12 elections. He posted the video on social media with the caption, “Ishraque's Action: Drug dens smashed and dealers handed over to the police.” The post also said he had previously conducted anti-drug raids in parts of his downtown Dhaka constituency and vowed to continue the campaign to make the area drug-free. Gendaria police station officer-in-charge Moniruzzaman Monir said officers went to the location after being informed that the men had been detained. “They detained six people and claimed they were drug abusers, so we went and brought them in,” he said. “Some powder was found in their possession, which will be tested to find out if the substance is a drug,” he added.

End of Article

title: Balochistan unrest: Teacher's killing by 'Pak-backed death squads' sparks outrage
text:
The alleged torture and killing of a teacher in Pakistan’s restive Balochistan province triggered protests by his family members and local residents, who warned that a key highway would be blockaded if authorities failed to take action. The protesters accused Pakistani forces of shielding those allegedly responsible for the death of Parvez Mazar, an Arabic teacher at Government High School Babbar Shor in Pasni, a coastal town in Balochistan’s Gwadar district, The Balochistan Post reported. According to Mazar’s relatives, he was "taken away" in front of his family on Tuesday and was found dead the following day. They claimed that members of a state-backed armed group, described as a “death squad,” took him to a private torture facility, where he was detained and killed. Protesters, including Mazar’s children, gathered outside the Pasni Press Club, demanding the immediate arrest of those responsible for his death. They demanded accountability and justice for the deceased teacher's family. The demonstrators warned that failure to address their demands would prompt them to stage a sit-in at Pasni Zero Point and block the Makran Coastal Highway, a key route connecting Gwadar with Karachi in Sindh province, Pakistan’s largest city and the country's financial and commercial hub. They demanded that state institutions take action against armed groups accused of abducting, torturing and killing civilians while allegedly operating under the protection of state agencies.

What are Balochistan's 'death squads'?

Baloch rights organisations and activists use the term “death squads” to describe armed groups they allege receive support or protection from Pakistani state institutions. These groups have been accused of targeting civilians, political activists and human rights defenders in Balochistan, a province long affected by an insurgency and a security crackdown.(With ANI inputs)

End of Article

title: Sugar-free ethanol? Oil companies change recipe, here's what's next
text:
Oil companies change ethanol recipe

The government is changing the way oil companies source ethanol for blending with petrol, with sugar-based raw materials being taken out of the latest procurement tender for 2026-27. State-run oil marketing companies (OMCs) will no longer buy ethanol made from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses under the tender. The move is aimed at keeping more sugar available for domestic consumption while ensuring that the petrol-blending programme continues. Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL), on behalf of OMCs, issued the tender on October 16, inviting bids for around 11 billion litres of ethanol for the period from November 2026 to October 2027. The requirement is linked to India's programme of blending 20% ethanol with petrol. "The Government of India has issued directions that sugar diversion for ethanol be reduced to zero for ethanol supply year 2026-27," the tender document said, as cited by PTI. "No offers have been sought for ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar or sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses in this quantity bid tender," it added.

What can oil companies buy instead?

With sugar-based ethanol excluded, oil companies can source ethanol made from maize, broken rice, surplus rice procured by the Food Corporation of India (FCI) and C-heavy molasses. However, maize-based ethanol producers will also receive a lower price. The procurement price has been cut from Rs 71.86 to Rs 68.86 per litre. The incentive paid for maize-based ethanol has also been reduced from Rs 5.79 to Rs 2.79 per litre. This means producers will have to work with a lower procurement price and incentive for maize-based ethanol, even as grain-based raw materials become more important for meeting the country's ethanol needs.

Why has the government taken this step?

The decision comes amid concerns over sugar supplies and rising prices. Poor rainfall in Maharashtra and Karnataka, two key sugar-producing states, has raised the risk of lower sugar output. India is the world's largest sugar consumer and has been using ethanol blending to reduce its dependence on imported crude oil. But sugarcane and sugar used to make fuel are also raw materials that can contribute to food supplies. When sugar production is under pressure, diverting them for ethanol can add to concerns over domestic availability. The government is therefore trying to balance the need for sugar at home with its efforts to reduce oil imports and emissions.

Will petrol blending be affected?

India has adopted petrol containing up to 20% ethanol, known as E20, as the nationwide standard. Ethanol is made from agricultural raw materials, including sugarcane and grains, and blended with petrol to replace part of the fossil fuel used by vehicles. The programme has also created a substantial market for domestic distilleries and given farmers an additional source of demand for their produce. The latest tender does not end ethanol blending. Following a police complaint, accused Asif was arrested after being shot in the leg during an encounter near the back gate of Lady Shri Ram College, while co-accused Hemant and Mukesh were also apprehended. The incident has triggered sharp scrutiny over civic administration and women's safety across public spaces in the national capital.

A nursing student, identified as Harini, was found dead under suspicious circumstances near her residence in Telangana. The student had returned to her native village during college holidays. According to information, her mother, Rajeshwari, left the house to visit a relative, leaving the daughter alone at home. Upon returning, the mother could not find her daughter. A search subsequently led to the discovery of her body lying behind a bathroom on the house premises, located between neighbouring structures. Injuries were noticed on her body, prompting police intervention and raising suspicions regarding the circumstances surrounding the death.

A tragic incident unfolded in Uttar Pradesh's Azamgarh following an eight-hour siege where a man named Arvind Singh shot dead his wife Babita, two priests, and his son. The incident occurred during a ceremony organised following his brother's demise. Upon returning home, the accused reportedly questioned the priests about their Aadhaar cards before opening fire. While two priests managed to flee, two others along with Arvind's wife were killed on the spot. Arvind subsequently held his three children hostage inside a room. Police personnel and family members attempted to negotiate his surrender, but Arvind issued death threats, shot his son, and opened indiscriminate fire on the police. In retaliatory firing conducted for self-defence and child rescue, Arvind was injured and later declared dead at the hospital alongside his son. title: Pak crowd welcomes T20 champions
text:
A political controversy has erupted following reports of 14 internal objections raised by Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi over decisions involving Form 6 voter registration, electoral database centralisation, software concerns in Goa, and voter restoration appeals in West Bengal. While the Election Commission stated that internal deliberations represent institutional checks and balances, the Opposition demanded the resignation and arrest of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, and the BJP defended the process as democratic functioning. In Delhi, students and alumni of Lady Shri Ram College protested to demand improved street lighting, CCTV surveillance, functional pink booths, and enhanced policing following an alleged gang rape at Aastha Kunj Park and an encounter near the campus. Additionally, Tamil Nadu witnessed a political confrontation between TVK and DMK over an alleged sexual assault case involving granite baron R Veeramani.

In Tamil Nadu, authorities continue the investigation into granite baron R Veeramani over minor sexual assault allegations, conducting premises raids, tracing financial transactions, and seizing electronic devices following recent arrests. Political parties debate administrative delays in earlier probes as widespread power outages lead Chief Minister Vijay to inspect the Tamil Nadu Electricity Board headquarters. In Karnataka, the Bharatiya Janata Party stages demonstrations demanding the resignation of Chief Minister DK Shivakumar over a finance department circular regarding unbudgeted schemes. In Kerala, Chief Minister VD Satheesan responds to opposition claims concerning ministerial overseas travel and chartered flights. Additionally, the bulletin details reported procedural differences within the Election Commission over voter roll processes, campus security protests at Delhi's Lady Shri Ram College, External Affairs Minister Dr S Jaishankar's bilateral meeting with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the United Nations General Assembly, US President Donald Trump's UNGA speech on Iran, and weightlifter Mirabai Chanu's Asian Games medal victory.

A political controversy has erupted over revelations that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi recorded 14 objections over 10 months during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise. The concerns included changes to Form Six for new voter registration, access to digital databases and voter deletions in West Bengal and Goa. The Opposition has demanded accountability and accused Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of acting autocratically. The Election Commission, however, said decisions were taken unanimously after internal checks and balances. The BJP defended the poll panel, saying differences during deliberations reflect democratic decision-making. Former CEC OP Rawat and Congress leader Abhishek Manu Singhvi have debated the constitutional and operational framework of the Election Commission.

A major scandal has emerged in Tamil Nadu involving granite mining baron Veeramani, who has been arrested alongside Shanti and Mahendra Simon for the alleged sexual abuse of minors. The case, spanning allegations dating back over two decades and a 2019 incident, centers on video evidence recovered from a pen drive. Earlier, police spent nearly five months investigating before claiming lack of evidence and unable to identify the victim, seeking case closure. Following intervention by the POCSO Court and a change of regime, police identified the victim and the residential premises within twenty days, leading to the arrests and raising critical questions over earlier investigative lapses.

Ahead of the Supreme Court hearing on the Bengal Special Intensive Revision matters, an affidavit filed by the Election Commission highlighted that thirty-seven lakh appeals remain pending out of over thirty-eight lakh total filings. With nineteen existing tribunals deciding only one lakh twenty-six thousand cases over six months, disposing of the backlog could take up to twelve years. The Election Commission suggested expanding tribunals to forty-two, aligning with parliamentary constituencies, and introducing software for remote hearings. The poll body also denied allegations of mass voter disenfranchisement affecting election outcomes, presenting vote margins against voter deletion data across constituencies.

A debate on student suicides and allegations of harassment in higher educational institutions brought together Professor Badri Narayan, Vice Chancellor of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, and student activist Deepti Shelar. Addressing questions on institutional accountability and mental health, Professor Badri Narayan pointed out the mission under the National Education Policy to build more humane and supportive university environments. He remarked, 'Data says that many in 10 years or 20 years, more than thousands, many thousands cases happen in educational institutions', stressing that faculty and peer groups must remain vigilant to identify distress early. Meanwhile, Deepti Shelar highlighted student unrest over alleged caste discrimination and demanded strict administrative accountability, including the immediate removal of officials accused of pressurizing students. Professor Badri Narayan noted that ongoing police inspections are probing circumstances, warning against rushing to conclusions as investigations examine whether issues stem from societal factors, opinion polarization, or mental health pressures.

In an interview, Dr. Himanshu Rai, Director of the Indian Institute of Management Indore, addressed institutional protocols regarding caste harassment allegations and academic malpractice. He emphasized the distinction between internal inquiries and police probes under the SC/ST Act, stating, "The solidarity is absolutely legitimate.
