title: T20 WC is a gift to the country: Gul
text:
In Tamil Nadu's Valparai, police have booked TVK leaders, including the city secretary, along with nearly 20 others under the Doctors Protection Act for allegedly threatening government doctors. The incident occurred after a five-year-old boy who sustained injuries in a leopard attack was brought to the government hospital for emergency care. According to reports, a group entered the premises, questioned the medical staff, and created a ruckus while essential treatment was being administered. Hospital authorities alerted the police after staff were obstructed from providing required medical aid, leading to an FIR being registered against the individuals involved.

Political developments intensify over the Election Commission row as CPM approaches the Cockroach Janata Party seeking a common platform against Chief Election Commissioner Ganesh Kumar. CPM General Secretary M.A. Baby has written to the CJP leadership urging them to join hands with opposition parties to build a united front. The outreach comes as CJP's 48-hour ultimatum demanding the CEC's resignation concludes, with the group mapping out nationwide street protests starting from Mumbai ahead of demonstrations in the national capital. The CJP is yet to take a final decision on the CPM proposal.

A Delhi court has remanded the alleged mastermind of the Rs 700-crore medical procurement scam to four-day Anti-Corruption Branch custody till September 29. The accused was arrested after returning to India from the United States, following non-bailable warrants and a lookout circular issued against him. Officials are establishing the money trail after the accused allegedly formed multiple shell entities in the names of domestic staff and tea vendors to manipulate procurement deals for state-run hospitals. The agency previously arrested the former head of the Directorate General of Health Services and doctors in connection with irregularities in medical equipment purchases.

In this India Today Special conversation, filmmaker Meghna Gulzar and actor Prithviraj Sukumaran discuss their film Daayra, addressing thematic complexities surrounding sexual assault cases, extrajudicial encounter killings, and growing public disillusionment with the criminal justice system. The discussion explores how systemic bottlenecks and an overburdened judiciary with millions of pending cases lead to public frustration, often driving societal support for immediate retribution and police encounters over constitutional due process. Reflecting on landmark events such as the 2012 Nirbhaya case and the 2019 Hyderabad police encounter, the creators dissect the moral conflicts faced by law enforcement and citizens alike. Prithviraj Sukumaran elaborates on his role as DCP Raman, explaining how the narrative juxtaposes violent crimes against women with retaliatory police actions to prompt societal dialogue without validating vigilantism or offering simplistic moral conclusions. title: Younis Khan retires from T20 cricket
text:
Supreme Court Senior Advocate Vikas Singh questioned the functioning and impartiality of the Election Commission of India amid the ongoing debate over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. He argued that the poll panel is a multi-member body and its decisions should be taken unanimously or by majority. Singh also questioned the EC's role in the SIR exercise, arguing that the commission does not have the authority to determine the citizenship of individuals. He said such powers lie with the Ministry of Home Affairs under the Citizenship Act. He further called for greater independence in the appointment of election commissioners, suggesting an independent collegium involving the Chief Justice of India. Former Chief Election Commissioner OP Rawat, Congress spokesperson Bhavya Narasimhamurthy and BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari debated the allegations surrounding the poll panel and CEC Gyanesh Kumar. Bhandari defended the EC and rejected opposition allegations as "source-based fake news", while Narasimhamurthy questioned why NDA chief ministers were responding to the criticism instead of the CEC addressing the public directly.

In this debate, former Chief Election Commissioner O.P. Rawat, Congress national spokesperson Bhavya Narasimhamurthy, and BJP national spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari discuss allegations surrounding the Election Commission of India and its leadership under CEC Gyanesh Kumar. Pradeep Bhandari defended the poll body, asserting that constitutional decisions under Article 324 require unanimity and dismissing opposition claims as source-based fake news. In contrast, Bhavya questioned why NDA chief ministers are issuing statements on behalf of a constitutional body instead of the Chief Election Commissioner addressing the public directly. Emphasising institutional integrity, O.P. Rawat stated, 'Election Commission must come out, answer every point, every accusation,' noting that winning or losing elections does not impact an institution's objectivity. Recalling the EVM challenge organised during his tenure, Rawat maintained that all three commissioners share collective responsibility and must engage openly with citizens to allay concerns and restore confidence.

Nationwide protests by opposition parties against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls lead the day's political developments, with the BJP defending the exercise. Former judges Justice Sanjiv Banerjee and Justice Gupta examine the constitutional validity of the electoral revision and the burden of proof placed on voters. The Supreme Court has taken suo motu cognisance of five rape cases reported in Delhi over five weeks and directed authorities to conduct safety audits of public spaces. The court also addressed concerns over street lighting and police patrolling. Reports from Delhi, Lucknow, Kolkata and Bengaluru highlight women's concerns over safety. title: 2009:Pakistan celebrate World T20 win
text:
The dispute over the control of the Trinamool Congress (TMC) has reached the Supreme Court after the Election Commission allotted interim party names and symbols to the Mamata Banerjee camp and the rebel faction led by Ritabrata Banerjee for upcoming bypolls. The Mamata camp challenged the poll panel's decision to freeze the original TMC name and flower-and-grass symbol, arguing that the Election Commission failed to adequately consider the party's organizational structure while taking into account claims from rebel leaders facing disqualification petitions. A separate petition was also filed by the Mamata faction challenging the State Assembly Speaker's delay in ruling on disqualification pleas against ten rebel MLAs, while also contesting Ritabrata Banerjee's recognition as the Leader of the Opposition.

Political tensions escalate ahead of the Nandigram by-polls following the arrest of Congress candidate Milind Pradhan. The Bharatiya Janata Party targeted the Congress over its allegations of political vendetta, pointing out that Pradhan has four pending arrest warrants dating back to 2007, involving three murder cases and one arms-related offence in Purba Medinipur. While the Congress has questioned the timing of the arrest right before the polls, the BJP maintained that election authorities acted upon complaints under the rule of law. The political showdown intensified following Trinamool Congress support for the candidate, as the matter moves towards court proceedings.

The electoral contest in Nandigram witnessed intense political friction following the arrest of a Congress candidate in connection with previous criminal cases shortly after receiving support from the Trinamool Congress. Opposition leaders criticised the timing of the police action, calling it an act of political vendetta and questioning the conduct of the authorities ahead of scrutiny. The Bharatiya Janata Party defended the arrest, maintaining that individuals facing criminal allegations must face legal proceedings and asserting that lawful actions against corruption and criminal conduct would proceed without exception.

The United States has announced an agreement concerning Greenland, aimed at securing long-term defence control and preventing adversaries from establishing military bases or making sensitive investments in the territory. The pact explicitly bars non-NATO nations from setting up military installations, directly countering potential security and commercial interests from Russia and China. Geographically situated close to Russia, Greenland offers strategic forward-basing advantages for American defence. Additionally, the arrangement permits US companies to invest in the territory and mine critical rare earth minerals, addressing international competition over essential natural resources. The White House and the US State Department outlined that the agreement provides permanent security capabilities in Greenland, ensuring no foreign adversary military presence

title: Pak has an edge over Lanka: Tanvir
text:
A political confrontation has unfolded over accusations against the Election Commission of India and the functioning of Electronic Voting Machines. Addressing the controversy, it was pointed out that opposition parties accept election victories as personal achievements while blaming the Election Commission and voting machinery whenever the public rejects them. The remarks highlighted past questions raised against constitutional institutions, including the judiciary and the Comptroller and Auditor General over its Rafale review, as well as characterisations of EVMs as black boxes. It was noted that all three Election Commissioners held a press briefing clarifying voter registration protocols and procedures relating to Form 6, which had also received scrutiny before the Supreme Court. The remarks underlined that violence, vandalism, and efforts targeting election headquarters undermine democratic conventions, asserting that attempts to cast doubt on electoral systems weaken the integrity of democratic bodies.

A political war of words has erupted after former Kerala Chief Secretary G.G. Thompson alleged that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, during a flight to Delhi in 2016, advised him to contest the 2019 Lok Sabha elections on a Bharatiya Janata Party ticket. Thompson stated that he promptly rejected the offer. Seizing on the claim, Congress leader Rahul Gandhi attacked Kumar, alleging that he previously recruited for the BJP and accusing the prime minister and home minister of making him the election umpire. Speaking on the matter, Congress MP Jebi Mather called Kumar a "chief conspiracy commissioner", demanding his arrest and immediate resignation over alleged misuse of constitutional office. Meanwhile, the BJP strongly dismissed the allegations as fabricated, questioning why Thompson maintained silence for nearly a decade and casting doubt over his credibility, with party spokesperson RP Singh alleging political motives behind the delayed disclosure.

A political controversy has erupted in Karnataka after a municipal council cheque worth 18,093 rupees bounced in Mandya district due to insufficient funds. The cheque had been issued by the local municipal body to cover advertisement expenses. Seizing on the incident, the Karnataka Bharatiya Janata Party mounted an attack against the Congress-led state government, claiming that the state is facing bankruptcy and severe financial mismanagement. The opposition party questioned the state finances, asserting that the government does not even have 18,000 rupees in its account. Neither the state government nor the local administration has issued a clarification on the cheque dishonour.

Aishwarya Rai made a rare appearance at Mumbai airport on Saturday, drawing attention with her new look. The sighting triggered social media speculation about a possible Paris Fashion Week visit, though she has not confirmed it.

title: Razzak hopeful of Pak victory
text:
A twenty-two-year-old sociology student from Guwahati University was found dead after being discovered unconscious at a homestay in Guwahati. Her boyfriend claimed she died by suicide by hanging herself from a ceiling fan, but police state his version is still being verified. Her father has alleged that she was sexually assaulted and that she had informed her mother about the assault before her death, while the boyfriend's parents have countered these claims. Family and friends staged a protest demanding justice and seeking the intervention of the Assam Chief Minister, while the Vishva Hindu Parishad has alleged murder.

Protests over an alleged rape claim at Lovely Professional University in Phagwara escalated into violence on the second day, with students blocking the Phagwara-Jalandhar stretch of National Highway 44. Demonstrators pelted stones and vandalised vehicles, setting a Punjab police vehicle on fire and leaving several personnel injured. Police registered an FIR and formed a special investigation team to examine CCTV footage, forensic evidence, and phone records, stating that no corroborating evidence has been found so far. The university administration denied the incident occurred, while authorities called in additional forces to assess and control the situation.

A massive rescue operation is underway in Faridabad after a three-year-old girl fell into an eighty-foot open borewell. The child fell inside while playing around 5:30 p.m. Relief, rescue, and police teams arrived at the site to take charge of the operation. Emergency responders are excavating the ground adjacent to the borewell to reach the trapped child. Fire brigade units alongside an advanced life support ambulance remain stationed at the location to assist. The victim's father stated that the borewell was left uncovered and demanded that authorities ensure the safe return of his daughter.

In an interview with India Today, former Chinar Corps Commander Lieutenant General Satish Dua detailed the operational planning, strategic doctrine, and tactical execution of the 2016 cross-LoC surgical strikes following the Uri terror attack. Recalling the loss of 18 soldiers at Uri, Dua revealed that then Defence Minister Manohar Parrikar authorized the retaliatory mission during operational briefings in Srinagar. Indian Army Special Forces crossed the Line of Control to strike multiple terrorist launch pads simultaneously north and south of the Pir Panjal range at depths of four to five kilometers from stand-off positions. Intelligence assessments indicated between 40 and 60 terrorists were neutralized, while Indian forces suffered zero casualties. Dua emphasized that the operation combined tactical military action with diplomatic maneuvering at the United Nations General Assembly, establishing a precedent of proactive deterrence below the nuclear threshold that shaped subsequent responses, including the Balakot airstrikes.

title: T20 WC: Second semi-final today
text:
A political rift has intensified between former allies DMK and the Congress party following sharp attacks over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) row. The DMK questioned Rahul Gandhi's silence regarding alleged voter deletions under the SIR exercise in Tamil Nadu, asking why he has not endorsed Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge's call for dissolving state governments formed after the process. DMK representatives accused Gandhi of remaining silent out of reluctance to upset Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Joseph Vijay and his party, the TVK, which entered an alliance with the Congress following the state assembly elections. The acrimonious split between the two long-standing allies has led to the DMK exiting the INDIA bloc and rejecting invitations to join alliance meetings and protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The DMK has pointed specifically to over one lakh vote deletions in the Kolathur constituency, where M.K. Stalin faced defeat, alleging that the Congress ignores issues in states where election results favoured its new political partnerships.

High drama unfolded in central Delhi as Congress leaders, including Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, staged a dharna inside the Akashvani Bhavan complex after being stopped from marching towards Nirvachan Sadan. Top Congress leaders and opposition MPs sought to meet the Election Commission of India and demanded the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. Delhi Police detained several Youth Congress and NSUI party workers near the gates to isolate the gathering and control the commotion. Confrontations were reported near the gates as leaders addressed media personnel through the grilles, alleging they were forcibly prevented from speaking and exercising democratic rights. In response, the Bharatiya Janata Party criticised the opposition agitation, stating the demonstrations undermine democratic norms and questioned Congress over allegations regarding voter list revisions.

Opposition MPs staged a protest near the Election Commission of India headquarters after being stopped approximately 50 yards away at Akashvani Bhavan in New Delhi. The demonstration, led by leaders from the INDIA bloc, followed a march that commenced from Parliament to question the poll body over the election process. Leaders claimed that around 13 crore votes were deleted and raised demands for the restoration of these votes, a return to ballot paper voting, and the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. Demonstrators alleged that official decisions regarding Form 6 favoured the ruling party, prompting counter-statements from the Bharatiya Janata Party and the Election Commission rejecting the claims. Security personnel, including Delhi Police and paramilitary forces, were deployed around Gate Number Four of Akashvani Bhavan to maintain order. While several opposition leaders were detained during the demonstration, others continued a silent sit-in under a banyan tree at the premises

text:
In this edition of Statecraft, anchor Geeta Mohan analyses key geopolitical developments across the globe. At the United Nations General Assembly, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defended strikes on Iran and displayed a Starlink terminal alongside references to pager explosions, amid a walkout by delegates and a cancelled meeting with Elon Musk. Meanwhile in Washington, US President Donald Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping with full ceremonial honours, agreeing to extend the bilateral trade truce by two months while strategic disagreements over Taiwan, artificial intelligence, and rare earths persisted. The broadcast examines the regional implications of potential US-China rapprochement for India and the wider Indo-Pacific. Additionally, the programme covers Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif evading questions on Lashkar-e-Taiba founder Hafiz Saeed at the UN, as well as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's new cabinet decree prohibiting face coverings in schools and capping non-Italian speakers at 30% per classroom.

A major political and institutional controversy has erupted over allegations of an internal rift within the Election Commission of India concerning the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process. The INDIA bloc and Congress workers launched nationwide street protests across multiple cities, demanding the immediate resignation and arrest of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The opposition has also approached the Supreme Court seeking criminal prosecution and the quashing of decisions related to the electoral roll revision, while the BJP defended the CEC. Former Chief Election Commissioner O.P. Rawat dismissed allegations of illegality, describing procedural issues as minor and stating that dissent among commissioners is natural. In contrast, former CEC S. Y. Qureshi termed the unilateral decision-making unprecedented and illegal, claiming genuine voters were deleted and calling for an audit and rollback of recent electoral rolls.

In an interview, former Chief Election Commissioner S. Y. Quraishi addressed the reported internal rift within the Election Commission of India involving CEC Gyanesh Kumar and fellow election commissioners. Quraishi stated that unilateral decision-making by a single individual within the multi-member body renders decisions invalid, remarking, "Any, all decisions taken by a single man, whosoever he may be, he may be the chairman of the Election Commission, but they're all illegal." He discussed opposition demands to nullify recent elections, noting that extensive voter deletions have compromised the electoral process. Quraishi observed that dissenting election commissioners face distinct operational pressures, citing historical instances where dissenting members were removed. Addressing public agitation and street ultimatums, he described the diminishing public trust in the commission as unprecedented. title: T20 WC: First semi-final today
text:
The Union Cabinet has approved Fairfax-backed Canada Inc. as the strategic buyer for a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank for 52,878 crore rupees, leaving the Centre and LIC with a combined 34% holding. While the government highlights the winning bid of 81 rupees per share above its fair value benchmark, the United Forum of IDBI Officers and Employees has sought parliamentary scrutiny over valuation and public safeguards. In foreign affairs, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is scheduled to visit Mumbai and Jamnagar rather than New Delhi, placing commercial energy interests and Reliance Industries' refining hub at the forefront amid friction over Russian oil purchases. Additionally, Yemeni Houthi rebels are reportedly seeking to manufacture long-range ballistic missiles using components seized from China, while in the US, a 19-year-old was arrested in Illinois over an alleged white supremacist plot targeting a Hindu temple.

On News Track, Marya Shakil reports on the Supreme Court taking a grim view of the INDIA bloc's march to the court premises against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the Special Intensive Revision process. The bench, headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, observed that nobody can browbeat the judiciary and that mob entry into court premises is impermissible, issuing notices to Rahul Gandhi, Mallikarjun Kharge, Akhilesh Yadav, Mahua Moitra, and other leaders. The top court also agreed to examine the de-notification of Jantar Mantar as a designated protest venue. Senior Advocate Mahesh Jethmalani evaluates the legal limits of challenging unanimous Election Commission decisions and questions the suitability of Jantar Mantar for massive demonstrations. The programme further debates the Delhi High Court refusing to halt a protest in Connaught Place, alongside severe political clashes triggered by Prashant Bhushan's admission calling for regime change, drawing sharp rebuttals from the BJP and responses from Congress.

A major political confrontation has erupted in Telangana following allegations of irregularities worth ten thousand crore rupees in the Singareni Collieries Company Limited. BRS working president KTR demanded an inquiry by the Central Bureau of Investigation or a sitting judge, alleging that the BJP and the Congress have colluded to shield the guilty. Meanwhile, the BJP responded by raising allegations surrounding the Kaleshwaram project scam, accusing both rival parties of being corrupt and working hand in glove. Dismissing the accusations, Congress MP Anil Kumar Yadav labelled KTR's claims as completely baseless, asserting that the state government is honestly delivering welfare schemes to the people while questioning the BJP's silence on the Kaleshwaram project.

title: Unhappy end to India's T20 WC tour
text:
Voting has commenced across the Dharapuram and Madurantakam assembly constituencies in Tamil Nadu, marking the first electoral contest following the 2026 assembly elections. The by-elections were necessitated after the sitting All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam legislators resigned from their posts and the party to join the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam. Polling began at seven in the morning as citizens queued up to cast their ballots. The three-cornered contest features candidates from the ruling Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam, the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam, and the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam. In Madurantakam, Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam candidate K. M. Kumaravel faces Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam candidate I. Paranthaman and All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam nominee Kanitha Sampath. In Dharapuram, Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam nominee P. SathyaBama contests against Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam candidate S. Suganya and All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam nominee K. Bhanumathi. The by-polls are seen as a critical test for the ruling government's four-month tenure, the main opposition's revival efforts, and the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam's leadership.

A political controversy has intensified over alleged changes made to Form 6 used for new voter registrations. The Election Commission dismissed allegations made by Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi, who accused Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of illegally modifying the form. The poll panel maintained that the form itself was never altered, citing an additional declaration linked to the Special Intensive Revision process, which it claimed had judicial approval. Meanwhile, the Supreme Court stated that it did not approve any modified Form 6 and sought relevant official records to examine who authorised the changes. The Bharatiya Janata Party accused the Congress of misleading the public, arguing that the apex court had not termed the form illegal. Experts and former officials also weighed in on internal commission dissent and administrative procedures, as records revealed that two Election Commissioners had earlier raised objections to the additional declaration document.

The INDIA bloc has escalated its confrontation with the Election Commission, with opposition leaders planning a march from Parliament to the poll body's office demanding the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The Congress has prepared a sustained nationwide campaign seeking his resignation and a re-examination of recent election results, while the Aam Aadmi Party has opted out of the protest. Announcing the phased 'Vote Bachao Desh Bachao' agitation, the party outlined block-level rallies and padayatras starting 10 October, village-level chaupals from 25 October, a mega rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan on 1 November, and six converging yatras on 26 November.

title: Hilarious quips and ‘100,000-volt’ energy: the hypemen (and women) redefining Afrobeats music
text:
For the 2015 freshmen cohort of the history degree programme at the University of Lagos, their classmate’s first-semester presentation was so captivating that they began calling him Toby Shang, after the 16th-century Chinese dynasty he had focused on.

His crowd engagement that day had been harnessed from his high school days as a ginger-man (energiser) in a three-man band and as a private tutor. By his final year at university, his viral catchphrases and infectious energy had resulted in a hit song, Shedibalabala. Today, he is one of the self-acclaimed “evangelists and pioneers” in the Afrobeats sub-genre some are now calling Afrohype or lamba.

“Even my mother calls me Shang now,” the 32-year-old, born Tobi Michael Adeyeye, said in an interview near the university’s lagoon waterfront, where he once emceed gatherings.

Since then he has hosted his own rave, released two EPs and run four editions of his School of Hype – a one-day masterclass with online mentoring that has launched several rising stars.

Hypemen neither sing nor rap entirely, but perform high-octane ad-libbed vocals “and onomatopoeic sounds” over fresh beats or popular instrumentals such as Dorime, a made-in-Nigeria version of 1996’s Ameno by the French group Era, a song that has become a continental nightclub classic. In response, nightclub patrons donate or spray money – the Nigerian custom of throwing or placing money on someone to celebrate them.

Hype is now omnipresent at wedding after-parties, raves and corporate parties. On Instagram, one teenage sensation is now known for recording 30-second hypes for birthday celebrants at the request of friends or relatives.

“Hypemen have the gift of the gab and fine mic control,” said the London-based doctor and cultural critic Dami Ajayi, who encountered one at a party in Tirana last month. “He used the spaces between lyrics for hilarious quips, many of which were frontally risque and misogynistic,” he said.

Despite being a male-dominated sub-genre, a few women have made their mark, such as the Yaoundé-based bikutsi artist Lady Ponce, known as the “100,000-volt lady” because of her energy. Other notable female figures in the scene include Deborah ‘Hype Queen Baddy’ Francis – an alumnus of Shang’s school who died in September – and the radio presenter Melody “M.I.A” Adigo, both from Lagos.

The art of hyping as it is known in west and central Africa has its roots in praise-singing and call-and-response music styles ingrained for centuries in Black populations on both sides of the Atlantic. In west Africa, this tradition took the form of oral historians known as griots. In the US, it was sustained by negro spirituals, sacred folk songs created by enslaved African Americans.

These styles laid the foundation for the atalaku (meaning “look here, look at me” in the Kikongo language of the DR Congo) tradition that came alive in 1980s Kinshasa, followed by today’s hype scene.

title: An extraordinary life: descendant welcomes biography of woman ‘gifted’ to Queen Victoria
text:
When she was seven years old, Bayo Randle’s great-great-grandmother Sarah Forbes Bonetta was presented to Queen Victoria at Windsor Castle as a “diplomatic gift” from an African king.

Victoria would go on to pay for Bonetta’s education, approve her marriage to one of west Africa’s wealthiest men, and become godmother to her eldest daughter.

But while Victoria took a genuine interest in Bonetta’s welfare, making the orphan a royal protege and meeting with her over the years, their relationship was part of a bigger agenda.

Now, as a biography is published – Becoming Sarah Forbes Bonetta: A Yorùbá Woman in Queen Victoria’s Court – Randle has spoken of his family history.

“I don’t think a human being, who has agency, could be ‘gifted’ from one to another, but had she not been gifted to Queen Victoria, would I be here today?” said Randle, a British-Nigerian barrister from London.

The new book, by a Canadian academic, Prof Henry Lovejoy, charts how Bonetta was brought to England by Frederick Forbes, of the Royal Navy’s West Africa Squadron, which was set up to enforce the abolition of the transatlantic trade.

Born in 1843 in Òkè-Òdàn, south-west Nigeria, Bonetta was originally called Àìná. Her family was killed in 1848 when her town was attacked by King Ghezo of Dahomey’s forces.

Bonetta, then five, is believed to have been captured by the agodjié – the all-female regiment depicted in the Hollywood movie The Woman King – and held at King Ghezo’s court.

In 1850, Forbes went to Dahomey – which is now Benin – to petition Ghezo to sign an anti-slavery treaty. The mission failed but Forbes asked Ghezo if he could take Bonetta to England.

Bonetta would go on to live a life of renown, becoming one of the most artistically represented and widely reported African women of her time. But she was never truly free.

Lovejoy’s book describes how, before Forbes arrived in England with her – giving her his own name and that of his ship, the Bonetta – he petitioned for her to be “the property of the crown”.

This meant Bonetta was “effectively indentured to Queen Victoria until age 19” under the post-abolition legal structures, Lovejoy said. Bonetta was then married off to James Pinson Labulo Davies, a merchant and philanthropist, of whom she would write: “I don’t feel a particle of love for him.”

Lovejoy’s research for the website liberatedafricans.org, developed with Kartikay Chadha, documents how, after abolition, more than 700,000 Africans “liberated” from enslavers were forced into indentures of up to 14 years “to pay for the cost of their own freedom” by governments including Britain’s.

Lovejoy claims Bonetta was at the elite end of this bonded labour system, “educated to be a missionary who would Christianise Africa”. In her lifetime her image was exploited as imperial iconography, promoting the idea that British colonialism of Africa was a “civilising mission”.

title: LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested
text:
Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report.

More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.

The intensifying crackdown comes as the law criminalising homosexuality in the country was toughened earlier this year. On 11 March, Senegal’s parliament amended the penal code, doubling the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years.

The new law introduced penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5m CFA francs (£650–£6,500) for promoting homosexuality, or supporting or financing LGBTQ+ people and organisations.

Larissa Kojoué, LGBTQ+ rights researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “LGBTQ+ people are being forced to curb their normal activities … for fear of arrest and increased stigma. Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.”

Same-sex sexual activity was criminalised in Senegal in 1965, but hostility towards LGBTQ+ individuals has grown in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, who ended up winning the election, and the former prime minister Ousmane Sonko promised to strengthen laws criminalising same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority.

Arrests of men and women have happened all over the country. The police say they have arrested people based on information extracted from seized phones, third-party allegations or raids on private premises.

The changes to the penal code have had a chilling effect on lawyers, who said they were afraid to represent people for fear of being prosecuted themselves, according to the report. Doctors told Human Rights Watch that the changes were discouraging people from seeking HIV testing and treatment.

While there was a 49% fall in new HIV infections in western and central Africa from 2010 to 2022, sub-Saharan Africa remains disproportionately affected by the virus, with 64% of all people living with HIV globally.

Sylvie Beaumont, a consultant with HIV Justice Network, said she had received anecdotal evidence that HIV clinics had seen a drop in attendance. “Obviously this is not good for the HIV response because people are going without treatment, they’re not going to get tested,” she said.

“The consequences are really bad and it’s sad because Senegal was a country that was doing well with their HIV response. They are shooting themselves in the foot.”

She said while the law criminalising deliberate HIV transmission was not part of the reforms to the penal code this year, there had been an “unprecedented” rate of arrests in recent months. She labelled the charges “nonsen

title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning story
text:
The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”

Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho.

Vara said that when she read the story, she “was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms”.

She said: “Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad – maudlin and full of tired tropes.”

Kundizeza responded in a statement on X: “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter’. I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work.

“I look forward to continuing to work with the Caine prize team, and to celebrating this recognition with the people who helped bring this story into the world. Most importantly, I will continue to write.”

Similar claims have been made recently about other literary prize winners. In July, the Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir won the Commonwealth Foundation’s short story prize with The Serpent in the Grove, despite critics on social media claiming it had “obvious markers” of AI writing.

Last month, the Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça Ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) was removed from the longlist of France’s most prestigious literary prize, the Goncourt, after an anonymous online account alleged the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.

The Caine prize said in a statement that it was reviewing the allegations that Kundizeza had used AI. It said: “When such claims are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process.”

Its chair questioned the reliability of AI-detection software itself.

Ellah Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row radio show: “As someone who chairs a prize, I’m obviously not against AI, but what I am against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case, regardless of what the Atlantic says, because they have already proclaimed our winner to be a cheater without investigating it properly.

“I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.”

title: Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns
text:
Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.

The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.

Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week.

But the health ministry never agreed to or authorized the trial, said Quinhin Nantote in Portuguese at a press briefing, where he referred to the study as “tests”.

“The ministry did not authorize the tests under the terms presented in the publications currently in circulation,” the health minister said. He said officials in Guinea-Bissau were “surprised” to see media reports that the country had given approval to the study.

“Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, ‌must ⁠strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said.

He spoke after convening an emergency meeting in Guinea-Bissau with the Bandim Health Project, the local ethics committee, the National Institute of Public Health (Inasa) and the Expanded Vaccination Program (PAV).

The Bandim Health Project is run by the Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, whose decades of research have been called into question in the past year.

The claims made in nearly all of their papers are “highly misleading”, said Charlotte Strøm, a Danish researcher who has co-authored research showing that Aaby, Stabell Benn, and their co-authors had no significant findings in 24 out of 25 studies and that they’ve chosen not to publish research that may not support their viewpoints.

“When researchers operate like this and abandon proper methodological rigor, they literally decide on the results themselves, and that is not science,” Strøm said, calling it “problematic, questionable [and] unethical”.

She added: “I believe there is serious cause for concern.”

Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, which he says shows that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight”.

Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about why the Danish ethics committee members were told the trial had been approved by local authorities and why it could not be held in Denmark.

title: ‘4,000 people minding our own business’: four decades on, Falklands again face a hostile Argentina
text:
A dozen local people and a uniformed military police officer (“Do you mind if I sit in?”) took their seats at the back of the handsome wood-panelled courtroom that doubles as the Falkland Islands’ legislative assembly. Outside, it was a typically blowy early evening. It may nominally be spring in the south Atlantic, but Stanley harbour, with its dark grey water speckled with historical shipwrecks, was a cauldron of swells and churn.

Six of the assembly’s eight members – five men, one woman – waited patiently at a row of desks and microphones. The heating had been turned up to just short of uncomfortable. Behind them, a portrait of King Charles. From the other walls, dusty photographs of governors, of varying popularity, gazed disinterestedly at the scene.

Proceedings started at the raised hand of a bored-looking young man wearing headphones in the corner. He was transmitting the question and answer session via radio across the dozen or so inhabited islands that make up the 778-strong archipelago.

It was not clear how many of the Falklands’ 3,600 residents were listening in from their farm houses out in the diddle-dee shrub that coats much of the islands, or in the front rooms of Port Stanley’s white clapboard cottages with the pretty coloured roofs; likely not on a par with the number who learned 44 years ago from the Falkland Islands broadcasting station that their lands had been invaded.

“There’s no turning back, we can expect them by dawn,” the governor, Rex Hunt, had said then.

But for those who did tune in on Monday evening, there was much to dwell on. Not so much the answers about the local internet contract or the consultation on the contentious plan for a salmon farm.

“I have another one for you,” piped up one enthusiastic quizzer with a heavy local accent, a West Country burr with a slight antipodean lift. That intervention prompted a little shuffling of tired bums. But a rather more significant announcement was to come.

Lewis Clifton, an assembly member who can date his family’s residence on the Falklands to the late 1870s, advised the islanders that an unprecedented economic war was being waged against them – a community no bigger than an English village – by a country of 46 million people.

“I am concerned that the level of Argentinian thrust this time has been at a different level,” Clifton said. “Perhaps a more vehement and belligerent tone than [seen since] 1982, because it has the potential to threaten our very economic development.”

Facing a downturn in his domestic polling and with an upcoming election, Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has legislated to criminalise companies and individuals involved in the Falklands’ nascent oil industry, and suggested the fisheries industry on which it currently relies for its prosperity could be next.

title: ‘Serious incident’ at Alberta military base causes deaths and injuries, Canada officials say
text:
People have been killed and injured after an incident at one of Canada’s busiest military training bases in Alberta caused a large fire, Canada’s defence minister said Saturday.

“I’m saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base,” defence minister David McGuinty said at a press conference on Saturday night.

McGuinty described the situation at CFB Wainwright as “active and delicate” with the fire being monitored very closely. “I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory”, he said at the press conference, adding that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in the investigation.

McGuinty did not provide casualty figures or details about what caused the incident. The Canadian Armed Forces and federal, provincial and local authorities were coordinating the emergency response, he said. The nearby community of Wainwright was providing hospital and firefighting support.

A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180 km northwest of Wainwright, told Canada’s national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as Wainwright’s healthcare facilities became “completely overwhelmed” by the number of people needing care.

“This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton,” Dr Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra hospital, told CBC news. “It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster.”

In an earlier social media post, prime minister Mark Carney said: “A serious incident creating a major fire has occurred at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta.”

“Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected,” he said.

The Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire crossed the base’s fence earlier Saturday and was spreading rapidly due to high winds. Firefighters from multiple jurisdictions were responding, and no evacuation order was in effect.

Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100 kilometers an hour. The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.

The Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, described the fire as “significant and tragic” and said it was affecting many military personnel.

Saskatchewan premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.

Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.

The Canadian conservative opposition leader, Pierre Poilievre, said he had spoken with Carney and the defence minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.

“Pray for Wainwright, everyone,” Poilievre said i

title: Mexican judge sentences three men to 158 years in prison for murders of Australian and US surfers​
text:
A Mexican ⁠judge ⁠has sentenced ​three men to 158 years ⁠and nine months in prison each for ⁠the murder of ​two Australian ‌brothers ‌and their American friend during ‌a 2024 surf trip to the state of Baja California.

The ‌defendants were declared guilty a week ​ago of homicide, aggravated robbery, robbery with violence and vehicle theft ⁠with violence, crimes committed against ​Australian ​brothers Jake ​and Callum Robinson, and ​their ‌American friend ​Carter Rhoad.

Rhoad and the Robinsons were shot dead in a suspected robbery while travelling through Mexico.

They were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked on 27 April 2024.

Their bodies were found days later in a clifftop well with gunshot wounds to the heads.

Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons.

Two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were also found guilty and have been sentenced.

The families of the victims followed the sentencing hearing via video link.

Prosecutors had requested damages of more than $100,000 but the judge ruled against it and said any compensation would have to be pursued through civil proceedings.

The brothers’ parents, Martin and Debra Robinson, travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September.

They have established a foundation in their sons’ names to carry on their legacy.

The Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation aims to “help people live bigger, shine brighter and love harder in their honour”.

Callum, the older of the two brothers, moved to the US as a professional lacrosse player and has been remembered for his loving nature and passion for the environment, having been involved in coastal cleanups.

Jake, a doctor, was set to take up a position at Geelong hospital after returning to Australia.

He has been remembered for his academic success, his passion for sport, particularly cricket and surfing, and his compassion.

Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.

Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while travelling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

title: Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote looms
text:
Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen to its lowest level since records began, new government data shows.

But whether this globally important success is maintained or reversed is on a knife edge ahead of a presidential election run-off on 25 October between two candidates with sharply different visions for the future of the rainforest and how that affects relations with the US under Donald Trump.

The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, fell behind in the first round of voting despite an impressive record in slowing the destruction of the Amazon while also reducing poverty and food insecurity. He is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro.

The Prodes satellite data series, which is considered the most accurate measure of deforestation, showed forest clearance in the Amazon fell by 41.8% over the past year to 3,335 square kilometres, the lowest value since the start of such measurements in 1988.

This beats the previous record low by 1,236 sq km, equivalent to an area the size of Rio de Janeiro.

Since 2022, the year before the start of the Lula administration, the deforestation rate has slowed by 71.2%, according to the data collated by Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research. This was largely as a result of stronger enforcement measures and state investments in environmental agencies.

The Brazilian states with the worst records in 2026 were Pará, which registered 33.9% of all Amazon deforestation in the year, Mato Grosso (25.5%) and Amazonas (15.7%).

However, even in those places the figures were down by more than 45% on the previous year. The state where the problem grew worse (up 0.4%) was Roraima, which is a Bolsonaro stronghold.

Outside the Amazon, the neighbouring biome of the Cerrado – an area of savannah – registered its lowest annual deforestation since 2001, at 5,516 sq km. This is significant as the Cerrado has long been treated as an area of environmental sacrifice, where soya and beef producers could clear more forest than they were allowed to do in the Amazon. Over the past four years, Cerrado deforestation has fallen by 48.4%.

These spectacular results, which brought some conservationists to tears, stand in sharp contrast to the 2019-23 term of Jair Bolsonaro, who oversaw a 59.5% increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying more than a million trees a day, through cuts to forest protection agencies, reduced implementation of penalties for environmental crimes, and verbal encouragement for illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers.

Bolsonaro was then convicted for attempting a coup but his son has vowed to release his father and let him take any position in government that he chooses.

The younger Bolsonaro has followed his father’s example in courting support from predatory landowners in the Amazon and other extractivist interests while ignoring the climate crisis in his manifesto.

title: Brazil’s Lula says he now backs lowering age of criminal responsibility to 16
text:
Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced that he now supports lowering the age of criminal responsibility for “heinous” crimes from 18 to 16, reversing a longstanding policy in what is widely seen as a desperate electoral gambit.

The U-turn, which Lula announced during a Thursday night interview with TV Globo, comes with the presidential runoff in just over a week. The incumbent faces an uphill battle to overturn the first-round victory of his opponent, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who remains slightly ahead at the polls.

Both the senator and his father, the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, have long supported lowering the age of criminal responsibility – they want it reduced to 14 rather than 16 – but Lula and his party have always opposed the change.

After repeated opinion polls, the latest of them this week, showed that 80% of the population supports lowering the age, Lula said: “My view, as a Brazilian citizen, is that for any and every heinous crime, I am in favour of lowering the age.”

He answered “yes” when the reporter asked whether he meant lowering it to 16.

The list of crimes classified as “heinous” under Brazilian law is extensive, ranging from murder and rape to the falsification of medicines and drug trafficking – the offence for which about a quarter of the 816,000 people serving prison sentences in Brazil were incarcerated.

Human rights organisations and security experts have long criticised proposals to lower the age of criminal responsibility, arguing that they do little to tackle violence while increasing recruitment into organised crime in Brazil’s overcrowded prisons.

On Thursday, before Lula’s interview, the proposal had been discussed in the senate. The Episcopal Conference of Brazil, a Catholic bishops’ organisation, had criticised it for “not addressing the causes of violence”, adding that placing young people “prematurely in the prison system tends to deepen cycles of violence and exclusion, undermining their rehabilitation”.

The columnist Josias de Souza wrote in his UOL column that, by reversing his longstanding position, Lula “decided to change himself. It was no ordinary transformation. On public security, Lula turned himself inside out. He began defending what he had always rejected.”

title: No 10 leaves option open to impose Chinese EV tariffs if UK joins EU scheme
text:
No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.

Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme.

The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.

The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.

The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”.

“We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.

This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.

However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.

Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.

They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”

Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.

EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.

But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.

Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.

According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.

title: Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed
text:
A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.

The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues.

While some low-resolution copies have been uploaded on blogs, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand said it had received several requests for the photos and had released the full set of 47 images in digital high-resolution format on its website.

The negatives were found more than a decade ago by Matthew O’Sullivan, the keeper of photographs at the museum in Christchurch.

Earhart’s most prominent investigator, Ric Gillespie, described the images as a “goldmine” in his blog, saying they were a complete set of aerial photos taken on 1 December 1938 by an amphibious biplane during a New Zealand survey of Pacific islands that was looking for suitable airbase locations.

What happened to Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan when they disappeared on 2 July 1937 during an attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator has been a stop-and-start search over eight decades, filled with false leads.

A leading theory is that the aviator, who broke several records including becoming the first woman to fly a nonstop solo trip across the Atlantic, ran out of fuel and was marooned on Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.

The hypothesis is that she survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating fish and turtles, based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and artefacts, including glass from a jar that is thought to have contained cosmetic cream.

This week, archaeologists and scientists from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University in Indianapolis, are searching a part of the island for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape in a lagoon named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image. Other longtime Earhart explorers, including Gillespie, are not convinced, saying it is probably a fallen tree and not the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. The small atoll has been visited dozens of times.

In their latest update on Nikumaroro, which is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, the expedition said severe weather had hampered their metal-detecting but that they would release an update within 48 hours.

“Despite Thursday’s weather delay, the expedition remains on schedule, with two more days of field operations planned – and an update on the identification of the Taraia Object expected,” Purdue University said.

Rick Pettigrew, the expedition lead and executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute, said: “We understand the tremendous interest in what we’re doing at Nikumaroro, and we appreciate everyone’s p

title: Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands
text:
Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction.

Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range.

Ore from the Cahaya and Hengjaya mines was traced through regional smelters and Chinese processing plants run by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, a cathode manufacturer that supplies CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. Huayou’s corporate reports list US and European carmakers as end-users, while additional corporate files and trade data show a separate route from Huayou to LG, a South Korean group that also supplies battery products to leading carmakers, via Poland.

Satellite analysis shows the mines have led to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by the indigenous Tolaki people.

“We used to ask the forest for protection in return for our offerings,” said Wadimula, a Tolaki elder whose home sits on the edge of the 21,000-hectare Cahaya mining concession. “Destroying it means destroying our own life.”

Electric vehicles are less environmentally harmful than fossil fuel-burning engines, which spew gases that foul the air and heat the planet, but western carmakers have struggled to clean up supply chains for batteries built with critical minerals from Africa, Asia and South America. Environmental groups warn that a failure to curb the boom of material-hungry SUVs is exacerbating the destruction by increasing the quantity mined.

Ore from the two mining concessions is sent to a nickel smelter in an industrial complex in Morowali, on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary, where limonite is refined into mixed hydroxide precipitate, the primary raw material used to make battery cathodes.

In 2024, $606m worth of mixed hydroxide precipitate was shipped from the Morowali plant to ports in China, followed by further shipments worth $470m in 2025. The processed ore was transported overland to Huayou cathode manufacturing sites in Quzhou, near Shanghai, and Yulin, near the border with Vietnam.

Public filings do not disclose specific volumes or timings of sales from Huayou to CATL, which would be needed to directly connect specific ore shipments to car batteries, but Huayou confirmed group-level supplies to CATL in response to a regulatory inquiry by the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 2024. Chengdu B&M, a downstream subsidiary of Huayou, has also confirmed the supply of “large quantities” to CATL.

title: Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debt
text:
An accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, as fears over rising inflation and future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.

Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5% respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.

Meanwhile, Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by 4.9% on Thursday, after an 11% slump in the memory chip maker Kioxia and a 10% drop in SoftBank, a big investor in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI.

The falls followed a slide on Wall Street during the previous day’s session, where the Nasdaq Composite fell by 1.9% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, its worst performance since July.

US stocks fell further when trading resumed on Thursday. The Nasdaq dropped another 1.4% at the start of trading, with Dell, which makes datacentre servers, and Coherent, which manufactures components for AI datacentres, leading the early fallers.

The sell-off came after US data on Wednesday showed stateside inflation jumped to a higher-than-expected 3.7% in September, marking the fastest increase in prices since the consumer price index (CPI) rate hit a three-year peak of 4.2% in May.

Fresh data on Thursday showing US producers increased their prices by 6.3% year on year in September – the sharpest rise since December 2022 – added to inflationary jitters.

The figures have rattled investors who are now expecting fresh interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, with some punters pricing in another increase as soon as the end of the month.

“Markets have just had an incredibly tumultuous 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print was then followed up with mounting fears around the AI trade,” Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid said.

Worryingly, the figures showed this was not about fuel costs, which have been pushed up by geopolitical tensions including the ripple effects from the US war on Iran. Reid said: “This wasn’t just an energy surge driving prices higher, as there were broad-based moves across the consumer basket.”

The sell-off follows warnings from the International Monetary Fund, which said this week that the threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets was putting world financial stability at risk.

“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” the IMF said. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, with the UK and eurozone potentially more insulated – although investors with US holdings would be hit.

title: Indonesia fights fire with dry ice as toxic haze spreads across region
text:
As fires ravage Indonesia, emitting a toxic smoke that has drawn the ire of regional neighbours, the government is testing an unusual new approach to tackle the haze: dry ice.

Having tried cloud seeding, water bombing and sending in army personnel to fight the fires, Indonesia’s coordinating security minister said dry ice would be dropped on the province of South Sumatra on Thursday.

“This trial of dry ice dispersal is being conducted under the president’s direct instruction to help tackle the haze in South Sumatra,” minister Dudung Abdurachman was quoted as saying by state news agency Antara.

“We will first observe the results, and if effective, there is a possibility that this method could be implemented in other regions.”

Since January, almost 900,000 hectares have been burned Indonesia-wide in the worst fire season in more than a decade, exacerbated by this year’s “godzilla” El-Nino and as the practice of “slash and burn” to clear land for crops such as palm oil persists.

For months, millions of Indonesians have been subject to thick smoke and an apocalyptic tangerine haze, with criticism mounting of the government’s response, including a class action lawsuit filed last week accusing it of “gross negligence”. Tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to the haze.

Air quality has also plummeted in neighbouring countries, shuttering schools, grounding flights and driving a spike in respiratory illness.

The haze has drifted into neighbouring Singapore, Malaysia and as far afield as the Philippines. Timor-Leste has said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from Thursday and urged families to keep children indoors or to use “respiratory protection” if going outside.

Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment starting on Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes occurred. The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents.

In the past week, the financial hub of Singapore was listed among the most polluted cities globally. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected, was at number two.

On Thursday, a Cessna aircraft will reportedly disperse 1.5 tons of dry ice over the South Sumatran city of Palembang, a move the government hopes will ease the smoke and improve air quality and visibility.

The technique was first deployed in the 1940s to promote ice formation in clouds, Bloomberg reported.

But experts say the use of dry ice, or solid carbon dioxide, might only offer local, and limited relief.

“It’s got some potential for local relief that might work for a while,” says Rick McRae, an adjunct professor from the University of New South Wales’ (UNSW) bushfire research group.

“Weather systems are all moving from east to west. So if you’re in a town under that and you clear the smoke, there’s gonna be more blowing all the time,” he says, “So it’s a constant … It’s not going to be simple and it’s not going to be a permanent fix in any way

title: ‘Many family stories’: Tim Winton’s Cloudstreet takes out ABC radio poll of top 100 Australian books
text:
Cloudstreet, Tim Winton’s sprawling Australian family epic, has been voted Australia’s favourite book in a poll run by ABC Radio National.

The broadcaster announced over the weekend the results of a nationwide poll to determine a list of readers’ top 100 Australian books.

Markus Zusak’s 2005 novel The Book Thief took second place, while Trent Dalton’s Boy Swallows Universe came in third.

First published in 1991, Cloudstreet follows two working-class Australian families, the Lambs and the Pickles, over their 20 years living together in an old rambling house called Cloudstreet, in postwar Perth.

The story – Winton’s fifth novel and ninth book – won a swathe of awards upon publication, including the Miles Franklin in 1992, and has been a staple of Australian English literature classes for decades. It’s sold hundreds of thousands of copies in Australia alone.

Cloudstreet has topped previous polls on Australian books, including one by the Australian Society of Authors surveying writers on their favourites in 2003, and a subsequent poll run by the ABC the same year, surveying the public. Winton’s novel appeared in a 2019 BBC list of “100 novels that shaped our world”.

The final top 100 in this year’s ABC Radio National poll included adult fiction, nonfiction, young adult fiction, children’s picture books, history and cookbooks.

The Australian Women’s Weekly Children’s Birthday Cake Book made it into the top 50 (at No 22), while Stephanie Alexander’s The Cook’s Companion came in at number 56. RecipeTin Eats: Dinner by Nagi Maehashi made the cut at 96.

Authors Helen Garner, Melissa Lucashenko, Geraldine Brooks, Anna Funder, Peter Carey and Hannah Kent all had multiple books in Sunday’s top 100. Books by children’s authors Alison Lester, Paul Jennings, Mem Fox, Jeannie Baker and Ruth Park appeared in the final 100.

The earliest published work was For the Term of His Natural Life by Marcus Clarke from 1874 (No 80). The most recent were Sally Hepworth’s Mad Mabel and Charlotte McConaghy’s Wild Dark Shore, both published in 2025.

Kate Evans, the host of ABC Radio National’s literary show The Bookshelf, said the list included “audacious literary fiction to historical accounts of who we’ve been and how we might understand all that complicated past, to joyful children’s books, Indigenous stories of both pain and humour, and many, many family stories”.

“This list defies any glib conclusions about how we read – and surely that’s the point,” Evans said.

title: Indigenous woman shackled to hospital bed while in labour in Queensland
text:
An incarcerated Indigenous woman was shackled to a hospital bed in Queensland while she was in labour last weekend, an advocacy group has said.

The birth happened just days before Labor and the Coalition blocked a bill to ban the “barbaric practice” of shackling incarcerated women during childbirth.

Debbie Kilroy, the chief executive officer of advocacy group Sisters Inside, said an Aboriginal woman who gave birth via caesarean section to a premature baby on the weekend and was still in hospital had been “shackled on and off since she came into the hospital”.

Hospital staff rang Sisters Inside after trying everything they could to get the shackles removed, she said.

“They were even crying because prison staff wouldn’t remove the shackles.”

A Queensland corrective services spokesperson said the incident would be reviewed.

“This incident will be subject to an internal review as restraints are only ever to be used as a last resort on pregnant prisoners where necessary to maintain public safety,” the spokesperson said.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Lidia Thorpe, a Gunnai, Gunditjmara and Djab Wurrung woman and independent senator for Victoria, introduced bills to the Senate this week to ban shackling and to stop children being strip-searched.

“[The] people sitting in this room have the power to end these barbaric, inhumane, traumatic and totally unnecessary practices,” Thorpe said.

As part of the UN, Australia has signed on to the Bangkok rules on the treatment of female prisoners, which state that prison should be a last resort for pregnant women and that “instruments of restraint shall never be used on women during labour, during birth and immediately after birth”.

But the government said this week the criminal justice system was a matter for the states and territories while the Coalition said it understood the intent of the bill but would not support its passage.

The Queensland Liberal senator Paul Scarr broke ranks to say he was “deeply concerned” about the practice and would raise it with the Queensland attorney general.

Kilroy said the woman in the Queensland hospital had been “spiralling” before the shackles were removed on Friday.

“As soon as she was shackled her health was deteriorating,” she said.

“Mum wasn’t running anywhere, mum wasn’t being violent.”

An inquiry into Thorpe’s bill heard about women having one leg and one arm shackled, with only one arm available to hold their newborn.

Thorpe said on Friday that “the Albanese government had the opportunity to take a stand against this barbaric practice”.

“Instead, they voted to allow it to continue. Not a day later, we hear of another harrowing case,” she said.

Thorpe said it was “a joke” for the commonwealth to leave it to states and territories because they “have the constitutional power to establish a national standard and they are choosing not to use it”.
